title: Museum of Indian History
welcome: Welcome to the Museum of Indian History. Six wings take you from the first stone tools, more than a million years ago, to India today. Select a glowing archway in the Grand Hall to enter a wing. Inside, select any board to read it and hear its story, and use Next to follow the guided tour. The directory and the visitor guide are in the two rooms beside this entrance.

wings.title: Ancient India
wings.subtitle: Prehistory to the Mauryas' eve
wings.intro: Welcome to Ancient India. Walk from the first stone tools through the cities of the Indus, the Vedic age, the new religions of the Ganga plain and the great states that followed.

sections.title: Prehistoric India
sections.intro: Long before writing, people in India made stone tools, painted rock shelters, tamed animals and began to farm. This section follows the Stone Ages and the Copper–Stone Age.

exhibits.title: Palaeolithic Age (Old Stone Age)
exhibits.text: The Palaeolithic, or Old Stone Age, is the longest phase of the human past. In India it begins with stone tools at least 1.5 million years old, such as those from Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu, and lasts until about 10,000 BCE, when the last Ice Age ended.
exhibits.show: Acheulean hand axes and cleavers from Attirampakkam, Tamil Nadu

exhibits.title: Lower Palaeolithic
exhibits.text: Acheulean hand-axes and cleavers, shaped by flaking large pebbles and cobbles, mark the Lower Palaeolithic. Their makers were early humans such as Homo erectus. Sites include Attirampakkam, Isampur and Hunsgi in Karnataka, and Hathnora on the Narmada, where a fossil hominin skull was found.
exhibits.show: Acheulean cleaver from the Hunsgi–Isampur valley, Karnataka

exhibits.title: Middle Palaeolithic
exhibits.text: From roughly 385,000 years ago, toolmakers turned to smaller flake tools: scrapers, borers and points struck from carefully prepared cores. Middle Palaeolithic sites are found across India, including the Belan valley, Bhimbetka, and Nevasa on the Pravara river.
exhibits.show: Middle Palaeolithic flake tools (scrapers, points) from Nevasa, Maharashtra

exhibits.title: Upper Palaeolithic
exhibits.text: The Upper Palaeolithic, from about 40,000 years ago, brought long, thin stone blades, burins, bone tools and the first ornaments, such as ostrich-eggshell beads. Modern humans, Homo sapiens, spread across the subcontinent. Patne in Maharashtra and the Belan valley are key sites.
exhibits.show: Engraved ostrich-eggshell fragments from Patne, Maharashtra (Upper Palaeolithic)

exhibits.title: Stone Age tools and technology
exhibits.text: Stone Age people chose fine-grained stones such as quartzite and chert. Over time they moved from heavy core tools to flakes and then to blades, getting more cutting edge from every stone. Wooden spears, bone points and the control of fire completed their tool kit.
exhibits.show: Comparative set of Indian stone tools: hand axe, scraper, blade and microlith

exhibits.title: Hunter-gatherer lifestyle
exhibits.text: Palaeolithic people lived in small, mobile bands. They hunted deer, wild cattle and pigs, and gathered fruit, roots and honey. They camped near rivers and in rock shelters, moving with the seasons. There was no farming, pottery or permanent village yet.
exhibits.show: Hunting scene rock paintings at Bhimbetka, Madhya Pradesh

exhibits.title: Palaeolithic sites
exhibits.text: Key Palaeolithic sites include Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu, Hunsgi and Isampur in Karnataka, Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, Didwana in Rajasthan, the Belan valley in Uttar Pradesh, Hathnora on the Narmada, and the Sohan valley, now in Pakistan.
exhibits.show: Map of major Palaeolithic sites of India (Attirampakkam, Hunsgi, Bhimbetka, Didwana, Belan valley)

exhibits.title: Mesolithic Age
exhibits.text: The Mesolithic, or Middle Stone Age, began about 10,000 BCE as the climate warmed after the Ice Age. People still hunted and gathered, but they used tiny stone tools, stayed longer in one place, and in some areas began to tame animals.
exhibits.show: Rock shelters of Bhimbetka (e.g. 'Auditorium' shelter), Madhya Pradesh

exhibits.title: Microliths
exhibits.text: Microliths are tiny stone blades, often less than five centimetres long, shaped into triangles, crescents and trapezes. Set in rows into wooden or bone handles, they made arrows, sickles and harpoons. They are the signature tool of the Mesolithic.
exhibits.show: Mesolithic microliths (lunates, triangles, trapezes) from Bagor or Langhnaj

exhibits.title: Rock art
exhibits.text: The rock shelters of Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, hold thousands of paintings, the earliest probably from the Mesolithic. Painted mostly in red and white, they show hunting, dancing, animals and scenes of daily life.
exhibits.show: 'Zoo Rock' painted shelter at Bhimbetka, Madhya Pradesh

exhibits.title: Early domestication
exhibits.text: Late in the Mesolithic, some groups began keeping animals. Bones from Adamgarh in Madhya Pradesh and Bagor in Rajasthan suggest early domestication of sheep, goats and cattle, a step towards herding and settled life.
exhibits.show: Adamgarh rock shelters near Narmadapuram (Hoshangabad), Madhya Pradesh

exhibits.title: Mesolithic sites
exhibits.text: Important Mesolithic sites include Bagor in Rajasthan, Adamgarh and Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh, Langhnaj in Gujarat, Sarai Nahar Rai and Mahadaha in Uttar Pradesh, and Birbhanpur in West Bengal. Several have yielded burials and workshops for microliths.
exhibits.show: Map of Mesolithic sites of India (Bagor, Adamgarh, Langhnaj, Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha)

exhibits.title: Neolithic Age
exhibits.text: The Neolithic, or New Stone Age, brought farming, herding, polished stone tools and village life. In the north-west it began early, at Mehrgarh around 7000 BCE. In other parts of India it appeared later, at different times in different regions.
exhibits.show: Polished Neolithic stone celt (ground stone axe) from India

exhibits.title: Neolithic agriculture
exhibits.text: At Mehrgarh, early farmers grew barley and wheat. Rice was cultivated in the Ganga valley, for example at Lahuradewa, and millets and pulses in the south. Farming produced surpluses that let people settle and populations grow.
exhibits.show: Neolithic saddle quern and grinding stone (e.g. from Mehrgarh or southern Neolithic sites)

exhibits.title: Animal domestication
exhibits.text: Neolithic communities herded cattle, sheep and goats. The humped zebu cattle of India was domesticated in the north-west, probably around Mehrgarh. In the south, Neolithic ash mounds formed where cattle pens were periodically burned.
exhibits.show: Terracotta humped-bull (zebu) figurine from Mehrgarh, Balochistan

exhibits.title: Neolithic pottery
exhibits.text: Pottery appeared during the Neolithic, first made by hand and later turned on a slow wheel. It let people store grain, cook food and carry water. Different shapes, colours and decorations help archaeologists identify and date cultures.
exhibits.show: Early pottery from Mehrgarh, Balochistan (handmade to slow-wheel wares)

exhibits.title: Permanent settlements
exhibits.text: Farming tied people to their fields. They built houses of mud brick, as at Mehrgarh, or pit dwellings, as at Burzahom in Kashmir, and stored grain in bins and pits. The village became the basic unit of life.
exhibits.show: Neolithic pit dwellings at Burzahom, Kashmir

exhibits.title: Neolithic sites
exhibits.text: Key Neolithic sites include Mehrgarh in Balochistan, Burzahom and Gufkral in Kashmir, Chirand in Bihar, Koldihwa and Lahuradewa in Uttar Pradesh, Daojali Hading in Assam, and Brahmagiri, Maski, Piklihal and Utnur in the Deccan.
exhibits.show: Map of Neolithic sites (Mehrgarh, Burzahom, Chirand, Koldihwa, Daojali Hading, Brahmagiri, Utnur)

exhibits.title: Chalcolithic Age
exhibits.text: The Chalcolithic, or Copper–Stone Age, saw farming villages begin to use copper alongside stone. In different regions it ran from about 3000 to 700 BCE, and many of these cultures flourished outside or after the Harappan cities.
exhibits.show: Painted Jorwe ware pottery (spouted jar) from Inamgaon or Daimabad, Maharashtra

exhibits.title: Copper tools
exhibits.text: Copper was smelted and hammered into axes, chisels, fish-hooks and bangles. Because copper was scarce and soft, stone blades stayed in use. The Copper Hoards of the Ganga–Yamuna doab include harpoons and human-shaped figures.
exhibits.show: Copper Hoard anthropomorph and flat copper axes from the Ganga–Yamuna doab

exhibits.title: Chalcolithic villages
exhibits.text: Chalcolithic farmers lived in villages of round or rectangular huts. They grew wheat, barley, rice, lentils and cotton, kept cattle, and made fine painted pottery, such as the black-on-red wares of Malwa and Jorwe.
exhibits.show: Excavated Chalcolithic house remains at Inamgaon (Pune) or Balathal (Udaipur)

exhibits.title: Chalcolithic burials
exhibits.text: In Maharashtra, Chalcolithic people often buried their dead beneath house floors, children sometimes in urns, with pots and copper objects beside them, suggesting a belief in an afterlife. The burials of Inamgaon are well known.
exhibits.show: Chalcolithic urn burial beneath a house floor at Inamgaon, Maharashtra

exhibits.title: Chalcolithic regional cultures
exhibits.text: Major Chalcolithic cultures include Ahar–Banas in Rajasthan, Kayatha and Malwa in Madhya Pradesh, Jorwe in Maharashtra, with sites such as Inamgaon and Daimabad, and the Ochre Coloured Pottery culture of the Ganga plain.
exhibits.show: Map of Chalcolithic cultures (Ahar–Banas, Kayatha, Malwa, Jorwe) with Inamgaon and Navdatoli

quiz.q: Which UNESCO World Heritage Site in Madhya Pradesh is famous for its prehistoric rock paintings?
quiz.why: Bhimbetka's rock shelters hold thousands of paintings, the earliest probably Mesolithic.

quiz.q: What are microliths, the signature tool of the Mesolithic?
options: Tiny stone blades set into handles
quiz.why: Microliths are tiny blades, often under 5 cm, hafted in rows to make arrows, sickles and harpoons.

quiz.q: At which Kashmir site did Neolithic people live in pit dwellings?
quiz.why: Burzahom in Kashmir is known for its Neolithic pit dwellings.

centre.show: Acheulean quartzite hand axe from Attirampakkam, Tamil Nadu (c. 1.5 million years old)

sections.title: Indus Valley Civilisation
sections.intro: One of the world's first urban civilisations grew along the Indus and the Ghaggar-Hakra rivers, with planned cities, drains, standard weights and an undeciphered script.

exhibits.title: Discovery of the Indus cities
exhibits.text: In 1921 Daya Ram Sahni excavated at Harappa in Punjab, and in 1922 R. D. Banerji at Mohenjo-daro in Sindh. In 1924 John Marshall announced a new Bronze Age civilisation, among the earliest urban cultures in the world.
exhibits.show: 1920s ASI excavation photographs of Mohenjo-daro under John Marshall

exhibits.title: Extent of the civilisation
exhibits.text: It was the largest Bronze Age civilisation in area, stretching from Sutkagen Dor near the Iran border to Alamgirpur near Delhi, and from Manda in Jammu to Daimabad in Maharashtra, with Shortugai in Afghanistan as an outpost.
exhibits.show: Map of Indus Valley Civilisation sites (Sutkagen Dor to Alamgirpur, Manda to Daimabad)

exhibits.title: Town planning
exhibits.text: Harappan cities were laid out on a grid, with main streets crossing at right angles. Many had a raised, walled citadel and a larger lower town. Houses opened onto side lanes, and standard bricks in the ratio one to two to four were used everywhere.
exhibits.show: Grid streets of the lower town (DK area), Mohenjo-daro

exhibits.title: Harappan architecture
exhibits.text: Builders used baked and mud bricks. Notable structures include the Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro, waterproofed with bitumen, large halls once called granaries, houses with courtyards and private wells, and massive city walls.
exhibits.show: The Great Bath, Mohenjo-daro

exhibits.title: Drainage system
exhibits.text: Almost every house had a bathing area and drains leading into covered brick sewers along the streets, with inspection holes for cleaning. This planned drainage was unmatched by most cities of the ancient world.
exhibits.show: Covered brick street drains at Mohenjo-daro or Lothal

exhibits.title: Harappan economy
exhibits.text: The economy rested on farming, herding, crafts and long-distance trade. Cities depended on surplus grain from villages, while specialised craftspeople produced beads, pottery, metalwork and shell objects for local use and export.
exhibits.show: Terracotta bullock-cart model from a Harappan site

exhibits.title: Harappan agriculture
exhibits.text: Farmers grew wheat, barley, pulses, sesame and cotton; the Harappans were among the earliest to grow cotton. A ploughed field was found at Kalibangan, and a terracotta plough model at Banawali. Rice and millets appear at some sites.
exhibits.show: Early Harappan ploughed field with criss-cross furrows at Kalibangan, Rajasthan

exhibits.title: Harappan trade
exhibits.text: Harappans traded across the region and overseas. Mesopotamian texts mention Meluhha, probably the Indus region. Harappan seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia and the Gulf, and carnelian, timber, ivory and cotton were likely exports.
exhibits.show: Etched carnelian beads of Indus origin found at Ur, Mesopotamia

exhibits.title: Weights and measures
exhibits.text: Standard cubical weights of chert followed a system that doubled from one to sixty-four and then rose in decimal steps. Measuring scales, including one made of shell from Lothal, show careful and consistent measurement.
exhibits.show: Harappan cubical chert weights

exhibits.title: The Indus script
exhibits.text: The Indus script appears on seals, tablets and pottery, with about 400 signs, mostly in very short inscriptions. It was probably written from right to left. Despite many attempts, it has not yet been deciphered.
exhibits.show: Inscribed steatite seals showing Indus script signs

exhibits.title: Harappan religion
exhibits.text: Evidence suggests reverence for a mother goddess, sacred animals and trees such as the pipal, and possibly a horned figure on the so-called Pashupati seal. Fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal hint at ritual, but without readable texts much remains uncertain.
exhibits.show: The 'Pashupati' seal from Mohenjo-daro

exhibits.title: Harappan art and craft
exhibits.text: Famous works include the bronze Dancing Girl and the stone Priest-King from Mohenjo-daro, square steatite seals carved with animals such as the unicorn, terracotta figurines and toys, and red pottery painted in black.
exhibits.show: Bronze 'Dancing Girl' from Mohenjo-daro (National Museum, New Delhi)

exhibits.title: Harappan technology
exhibits.text: Harappans worked copper and bronze, made glazed faience, drilled long carnelian beads with special drills, and fired bricks in kilns. Lothal had a large brick basin often interpreted as a dockyard, though some scholars see it as a reservoir.
exhibits.show: Long carnelian beads and bead-drilling evidence from Chanhudaro/Harappa

exhibits.title: Harappan society
exhibits.text: Society seems to have included farmers, artisans, merchants and perhaps priests. Differences in house size and burial goods suggest some inequality, but no grand palaces or royal tombs have been found.
exhibits.show: Harappan terracotta figurines and toys from Harappa/Mohenjo-daro

exhibits.title: Harappan administration
exhibits.text: Uniform bricks, weights, seals and town plans across a vast area suggest strong coordination, perhaps by merchant or priestly elites or city councils. No palaces, kings or armies have been clearly identified.
exhibits.show: 'Priest-King' steatite bust from Mohenjo-daro (National Museum of Pakistan, Karachi)

exhibits.title: Major Harappan cities
exhibits.text: More than a thousand Harappan sites are known, but a few large cities stand out: Harappa, Mohenjo-daro and Ganweriwala in Pakistan, and Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Lothal and Kalibangan in India.
exhibits.show: Map of major Harappan cities (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Ganweriwala, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi, Lothal, Kalibangan)

exhibits.title: Harappa
exhibits.text: On the Ravi river in Punjab, Pakistan, Harappa was the first site excavated, in 1921, and gave its name to the civilisation. It had a citadel, rows of workers' houses, working platforms and large storage halls.
exhibits.show: Mounds and brick structures of Harappa, Punjab, Pakistan

exhibits.title: Mohenjo-daro
exhibits.text: On the Indus in Sindh, Pakistan, Mohenjo-daro was one of the largest cities, perhaps home to forty thousand people. Its Great Bath, grid streets and drains are famous, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its name means mound of the dead.
exhibits.show: Citadel mound with Buddhist stupa, Mohenjo-daro, Sindh

exhibits.title: Dholavira
exhibits.text: On Khadir island in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, Dholavira was divided into three parts and had remarkable water reservoirs cut into the rock. A large signboard of ten Indus signs was found near a gateway. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
exhibits.show: Rock-cut reservoir (eastern reservoir) at Dholavira, Gujarat

exhibits.title: Lothal
exhibits.text: Near the Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat, Lothal was a port and bead-making centre with a large brick basin, a warehouse and evidence of sea trade. It was excavated by S. R. Rao from 1955.
exhibits.show: Brick dock basin at Lothal, Gujarat

exhibits.title: Kalibangan
exhibits.text: On the Ghaggar river in Rajasthan, Kalibangan has the earliest ploughed field known, from the Early Harappan phase, as well as fire altars and a citadel. Its name means black bangles.
exhibits.show: Fire altars at Kalibangan, Rajasthan

exhibits.title: Rakhigarhi
exhibits.text: In Haryana, Rakhigarhi is among the largest Harappan sites. Ancient DNA from a woman buried there, published in 2019, offered new evidence about the ancestry of the Harappan people.
exhibits.show: Excavated mounds and burials at Rakhigarhi, Haryana

exhibits.title: Why did the cities decline?
exhibits.text: From about 1900 BCE the cities declined. Explanations include climate change and weaker monsoons, the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra river, shifting rivers and floods, and the collapse of trade. The once-popular idea of an Aryan invasion is no longer accepted as the cause.
exhibits.show: Map of the Ghaggar-Hakra palaeochannel with late Harappan sites

quiz.q: Which Harappan site, in the Rann of Kutch, had rock-cut reservoirs and a large signboard of Indus signs?
quiz.why: Dholavira on Khadir island had remarkable reservoirs and a ten-sign signboard near a gateway.

quiz.q: Where was the earliest known ploughed field found?
quiz.why: Kalibangan in Rajasthan has a ploughed field from the Early Harappan phase.

quiz.q: What is the current status of the Indus script?
options: It has not yet been deciphered
It was deciphered by John Marshall in 1924
It is an early form of Brahmi
It was read using a bilingual inscription from Mesopotamia
quiz.why: Despite many attempts, the roughly 400-sign Indus script remains undeciphered.

centre.show: Unicorn seal from Mohenjo-daro (steatite stamp seal with Indus script)

sections.title: Vedic Period
sections.intro: The Vedas, India's oldest texts, describe a world of cattle herders becoming farmers, tribes becoming kingdoms, and ideas about ritual, society and the self that shaped later Indian thought.

exhibits.title: Early Vedic Period
exhibits.text: The Early, or Rigvedic, period, about 1500 to 1000 BCE, is known mainly from the Rigveda. Its people lived in the land of seven rivers, the Sapta Sindhu, in present-day Punjab, north-west India and Afghanistan.
exhibits.show: Map of the Sapta Sindhu region of the Rigveda

exhibits.title: Who were the Aryans?
exhibits.text: In the Rigveda, arya means noble, a cultural and linguistic term. Most scholars hold that Indo-Aryan-speaking groups migrated into north-west India around 1500 BCE and mixed with local peoples; others argue for an indigenous origin. The debate continues.
exhibits.show: Map of Indo-European language spread / Indo-Aryan migration

exhibits.title: Rigveda
exhibits.text: The Rigveda, the oldest Veda, has 1,028 hymns in ten books, or mandalas, addressed to gods such as Indra, Agni and Soma. Passed down orally with great precision for centuries, its manuscripts are on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.
exhibits.show: Rigveda manuscript in Devanagari (BORI Pune collection, UNESCO Memory of the World)

exhibits.title: Tribal organisation
exhibits.text: Society was organised in kin-based tribes, or jana, led by a chief called the rajan, whose main duty was to protect cattle and people. Assemblies such as the sabha and samiti advised him, and women could attend some assemblies.
exhibits.show: Map of Rigvedic tribes (Bharatas, Purus and others)

exhibits.title: Early Vedic economy
exhibits.text: The early Vedic economy was largely pastoral. Cattle were the main wealth and wars were fought over them; gavishti, the search for cows, meant battle. There was also some barley farming, weaving, carpentry and work in copper and bronze.
exhibits.show: Early 20th-century photograph of cattle herders in north-west India (illustrative)

exhibits.title: Early Vedic religion
exhibits.text: Rigvedic people worshipped the forces of nature: Indra, god of thunder and war; Agni, fire; Varuna, guardian of cosmic order; and Soma. Worship centred on hymns and offerings into fire. There were no temples or images.
exhibits.show: Relief of Indra on his elephant Airavata, Bhaja caves, Maharashtra (c. 2nd–1st century BCE)

exhibits.title: Later Vedic Period
exhibits.text: The Later Vedic period, about 1000 to 600 BCE, is known from the later Vedas, the Brahmanas and the Upanishads. Settlement moved east into the Ganga plain, and society became more agricultural, hierarchical and focused on ritual.
exhibits.show: Painted Grey Ware bowl from the Ganga–Yamuna doab (e.g. Hastinapur, Ahichchhatra)

exhibits.title: Vedic expansion eastward
exhibits.text: People moved from Punjab into the Ganga–Yamuna doab and on to Kosala and Videha. The Painted Grey Ware culture of this region, found at sites such as Hastinapur and Ahichchhatra, is linked with this period.
exhibits.show: Map of Later Vedic expansion: Kuru–Panchala to Kosala–Videha

exhibits.title: Iron technology
exhibits.text: Iron, called krishna ayas, the black metal, came into wider use from about 1000 BCE. Iron tools helped clear forests and till the land, and iron weapons strengthened rulers.
exhibits.show: Early Iron Age iron tools (sickle, axe, arrowheads) from Ganga-valley sites

exhibits.title: Later Vedic agriculture
exhibits.text: Farming became the main occupation. Texts mention heavy ploughs drawn by many oxen, and crops such as rice, called vrihi, wheat and barley. Agricultural surplus supported larger settlements and rulers.
exhibits.show: Historic photograph of bullock-drawn ploughing in the Ganga plain

exhibits.title: Later Vedic social hierarchy
exhibits.text: The four varnas became more rigid and increasingly fixed by birth. Brahmins and kshatriyas claimed privileged positions, while shudras were placed at the bottom. Women's status declined compared with the earlier period.
exhibits.show: 19th-century Company painting of Brahmin priests performing a sacrifice

exhibits.title: Later Vedic kingship
exhibits.text: Tribal chiefdoms grew into territorial kingdoms called janapadas. Kings performed grand sacrifices such as the Rajasuya and Ashvamedha to assert power, collected tribute called bali, and were helped by officials. The sabha and samiti lost importance.
exhibits.show: Samudragupta 'Ashvamedha' gold coin showing the sacrificial horse

exhibits.title: Vedic Literature
exhibits.text: Vedic literature is shruti, that which is heard. It was memorised and recited for centuries before it was written down. It includes the four Vedas, each with its Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads.
exhibits.show: Students reciting Vedas in a traditional pathashala (oral tradition, UNESCO Intangible Heritage)

exhibits.title: The four Vedas
exhibits.text: The four Vedas are the Rigveda of hymns, the Samaveda of melodies for chanting, the Yajurveda of sacrificial formulas, and the Atharvaveda of spells, charms and everyday concerns. The tradition of Vedic chanting is recognised by UNESCO as intangible heritage.
exhibits.show: Samaveda manuscript with musical notation marks

exhibits.title: Brahmanas
exhibits.text: The Brahmanas are prose texts explaining the meaning and correct performance of sacrifices. The Shatapatha Brahmana is among the most important, and records social and geographical details of its time.
exhibits.show: Shatapatha Brahmana manuscript folio

exhibits.title: Aranyakas
exhibits.text: The Aranyakas, or forest texts, were meant for study in seclusion. They move from outward ritual towards symbolic and mystical interpretation, bridging the Brahmanas and the Upanishads.
exhibits.show: Pahari or Rajput miniature of rishis at a forest hermitage (ashram)

exhibits.title: Upanishads
exhibits.text: The Upanishads, over a hundred in number with about thirteen principal ones, explore the self, or atman, ultimate reality, or brahman, karma and liberation. They form Vedanta, the end of the Vedas. India's motto, Satyameva Jayate, comes from the Mundaka Upanishad.
exhibits.show: Upanishad manuscript folio in Devanagari (e.g. Isha Upanishad)

exhibits.title: Varna system
exhibits.text: The Purusha Sukta of the Rigveda names four varnas: brahmin, kshatriya, vaishya and shudra. At first more flexible, the system hardened over time into a birth-based hierarchy that shaped Indian society for centuries.
exhibits.show: Manuscript folio of the Purusha Sukta (Rigveda 10.90)

exhibits.title: Ashrama system
exhibits.text: Later texts describe four stages of life for men of the upper varnas: brahmacharya, the student; grihastha, the householder; vanaprastha, retreat to the forest; and sannyasa, renunciation. It was an ideal rather than a universal practice.
exhibits.show: Mughal/Rajput miniature of ascetics (sannyasis) at a hermitage

quiz.q: How many hymns does the Rigveda contain?
quiz.why: The Rigveda has 1,028 hymns arranged in ten mandalas.

quiz.q: India's national motto, Satyameva Jayate, comes from which text?
quiz.why: Satyameva Jayate is taken from the Mundaka Upanishad.

quiz.q: In the Rigveda, what did the word gavishti, 'the search for cows', come to mean?
quiz.why: Cattle were the main wealth, so gavishti meant war fought over cattle.

centre.show: Brick Vedic fire altar (vedi with sacred fire), as recorded at the 1975 Agnicayana in Panjal, Kerala

sections.title: Religious Movements
sections.intro: In the cities of the Ganga plain, new teachers questioned ritual and caste and offered paths to liberation through ethics and insight. Jainism and Buddhism grew into world religions.

exhibits.title: Jainism
exhibits.text: Jainism teaches that the soul can be freed through right faith, right knowledge and right conduct. Jains revere twenty-four tirthankaras, or ford-makers; the first was Rishabhanatha, the twenty-third Parshvanatha and the twenty-fourth Mahavira.
exhibits.show: Seated Jain tirthankara (Jina) in meditation, Mathura, Kushan period

exhibits.title: Mahavira
exhibits.text: Vardhamana Mahavira was born, according to tradition, around 599 BCE near Vaishali in Bihar, though some scholars place him later. After twelve years of austerity he attained kevala jnana, perfect knowledge, and taught for about thirty years before his death at Pavapuri.
exhibits.show: Kalpasutra manuscript painting of Mahavira (Western Indian style, 15th c.)

exhibits.title: Teachings of Mahavira
exhibits.text: Mahavira taught five vows: ahimsa, non-violence; satya, truth; asteya, not stealing; aparigraha, non-possession; and brahmacharya, chastity. Jainism also teaches anekantavada, the idea that truth has many sides.
exhibits.show: Official Jain emblem (Jain prateek, 1975) with the ahimsa hand

exhibits.title: Jain sects
exhibits.text: Jainism divided into the Digambaras, the sky-clad, whose monks renounce clothing, and the Shvetambaras, the white-clad. Tradition links the split to a famine in Magadha and the migration of the monk Bhadrabahu's followers to the south.
exhibits.show: Gommateshwara (Bahubali) statue, Shravanabelagola, Karnataka

exhibits.title: Spread of Jainism
exhibits.text: Jainism found support among merchants and rulers, including, by tradition, Chandragupta Maurya, and later Kharavela of Kalinga. It spread to Karnataka, Gujarat and Rajasthan, with great centres such as Shravanabelagola and Mount Abu.
exhibits.show: Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela, Udayagiri caves, Odisha

exhibits.title: Buddhism
exhibits.text: Buddhism, founded by Gautama Buddha around the 5th century BCE, teaches a path to end suffering through wisdom, ethics and meditation. It rejected sacrificial ritual and privilege by birth, and spread across Asia.
exhibits.show: Seated Buddha preaching the first sermon, Sarnath (Gupta, 5th c. CE), Sarnath Museum

exhibits.title: Gautama Buddha
exhibits.text: Siddhartha Gautama was born at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal, into the Shakya clan. He left home at twenty-nine, attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya, gave his first sermon at Sarnath and died at Kushinagar at the age of eighty.
exhibits.show: Mahabodhi Temple, Bodh Gaya, Bihar

exhibits.title: Four Noble Truths
exhibits.text: The Buddha's first teaching: life involves suffering, or dukkha; suffering arises from craving; suffering can end, in nirvana; and the way to end it is the Noble Eightfold Path.
exhibits.show: Dhamek Stupa, Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh

exhibits.title: Eightfold Path
exhibits.text: The Middle Way between luxury and harsh austerity: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration, grouped as wisdom, ethics and meditation.
exhibits.show: Eight-spoked dharmachakra in early Buddhist relief (e.g. Amaravati or Sanchi)

exhibits.title: Buddhist councils
exhibits.text: Four major councils preserved and debated the teachings: at Rajagriha after the Buddha's death, at Vaishali about a century later, at Pataliputra under Ashoka, and in Kashmir under Kanishka, which is linked with the rise of Mahayana.
exhibits.show: Saptaparni cave, Rajgir, Bihar (traditional site of the First Council)

exhibits.title: Buddhist schools
exhibits.text: Theravada, the teaching of the elders, spread to Sri Lanka and South-East Asia. Mahayana, the great vehicle, emphasised the bodhisattva ideal and spread to China, Korea and Japan. Vajrayana developed later in Tibet and the Himalaya.
exhibits.show: Bodhisattva Padmapani mural, Ajanta Cave 1

exhibits.title: Spread of Buddhism
exhibits.text: Royal patronage, especially from Ashoka, together with monasteries, trade routes and missionaries, carried Buddhism to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, China and South-East Asia. Great monasteries such as Nalanda became centres of learning.
exhibits.show: Map of the spread of Buddhism across Asia

exhibits.title: Other Shramana traditions
exhibits.text: Many wandering ascetics, the shramanas, questioned Vedic ritual. They included the Ajivikas led by Makkhali Gosala, who believed in fate, or niyati, and the materialist Charvaka or Lokayata school, which denied rebirth and the afterlife.
exhibits.show: Lomas Rishi cave, Barabar Hills, Bihar (caves dedicated to the Ajivikas)

quiz.q: Where did the Buddha give his first sermon?
quiz.why: He attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and gave his first sermon at Sarnath.

quiz.q: Who was the twenty-fourth Jain tirthankara?
quiz.why: Mahavira was the 24th tirthankara; Parshvanatha was the 23rd.

quiz.q: Which Jain sect's monks renounce clothing?
quiz.why: Digambara means sky-clad; Shvetambaras are white-clad.

centre.show: The Great Stupa (Stupa 1), Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh

sections.title: Mahajanapadas
sections.intro: Sixteen great states, some ruled by kings and some by assemblies, competed in the Ganga plain. Out of this contest Magadha rose to build India's first empire.

exhibits.title: Sixteen Mahajanapadas
exhibits.text: Buddhist and Jain texts list sixteen great states, or mahajanapadas, around the 6th century BCE, among them Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa, Avanti, Kashi, Anga, Vajji, Malla, Kuru, Panchala, Gandhara, Kamboja, Chedi, Matsya, Surasena and Assaka.
exhibits.show: Map of the sixteen Mahajanapadas

exhibits.title: Gana-sanghas: the republics
exhibits.text: Some states, called gana-sanghas, were governed by assemblies of clan heads rather than a single king. The Vajji confederacy, with its capital at Vaishali, and the Mallas were prominent. Both the Buddha and Mahavira came from such clans.
exhibits.show: Ashokan pillar with lion capital at Kolhua, Vaishali, Bihar

exhibits.title: Monarchies
exhibits.text: Most mahajanapadas, such as Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti, were monarchies. Kings collected taxes, kept armies and officials, and built fortified capitals such as Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi and Ujjain.
exhibits.show: Cyclopean wall of Rajgir (Rajagriha), Bihar

exhibits.title: Rise of Magadha
exhibits.text: Magadha, in Bihar, became the most powerful state thanks to fertile land, iron ore, rivers for transport, elephants and able rulers: Bimbisara and Ajatashatru of the Haryanka dynasty, then the Shishunagas and the Nandas. Pataliputra became its capital.
exhibits.show: Map of Magadha's expansion under Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and the Nandas

exhibits.title: Political and economic change
exhibits.text: This age saw the second urbanisation of the Ganga plain, punch-marked silver coins, standing armies, regular land revenue and growing trade, laying the foundations for India's first empire.
exhibits.show: Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) dish or bowl

quiz.q: How many great states, or mahajanapadas, do Buddhist and Jain texts list?
quiz.why: The texts list sixteen mahajanapadas around the 6th century BCE.

quiz.q: Which confederacy, with its capital at Vaishali, was a prominent gana-sangha?
quiz.why: The Vajji confederacy at Vaishali was governed by an assembly of clan heads.

quiz.q: Which dynasty did Bimbisara and Ajatashatru of Magadha belong to?
quiz.why: Bimbisara and Ajatashatru were Haryanka rulers, followed by the Shishunagas and Nandas.

centre.show: Silver punch-marked karshapana coin of Magadha

sections.title: Persian and Greek Invasions
sections.intro: The north-west of the subcontinent came into contact with the Persian empire and with Alexander of Macedon, opening routes for trade, art and ideas.

exhibits.title: The Persian Achaemenid Empire
exhibits.text: In the late 6th century BCE Darius the First of Persia conquered Gandhara and the Indus region, which became a province paying rich tribute. Persian contact brought the Aramaic script, from which Kharosthi developed, and influenced later Mauryan art and administration.
exhibits.show: Indian (Hindush) tribute-bearers on the Apadana staircase reliefs, Persepolis

exhibits.title: Alexander's invasion
exhibits.text: In 326 BCE Alexander of Macedon crossed the Indus and defeated King Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes, on the Jhelum. But his weary army refused to go beyond the Beas. He withdrew, and died in Babylon in 323 BCE.
exhibits.show: Alexander's 'Porus medallion' silver decadrachm (horseman attacking an elephant)

exhibits.title: Effects of Greek contact
exhibits.text: Alexander's campaign was brief, but it opened routes between India and the Greek world. Greek writers described India, Greek settlements remained in the north-west, and Greek influence later shaped Gandhara art and Indian coinage.
exhibits.show: Gandhara standing Buddha in Greco-Buddhist style (2nd–3rd c. CE)

quiz.q: Which Persian king conquered Gandhara and the Indus region in the late 6th century BCE?
quiz.why: Darius I made the region a tribute-paying province of the Achaemenid empire.

quiz.q: Which king did Alexander defeat at the Battle of the Hydaspes in 326 BCE?
quiz.why: Alexander defeated Porus on the Jhelum (Hydaspes).

quiz.q: Beyond which river did Alexander's army refuse to march?
quiz.why: His weary army refused to go beyond the Beas, so he withdrew.

centre.show: Achaemenid stone column with double-bull capital, Persepolis (Apadana)

wings.title: Classical India
wings.subtitle: Mauryas to the post-Gupta kingdoms
wings.intro: Welcome to Classical India: the Maurya and Gupta empires, the kingdoms of the Deccan and the far south, and the trade and art that linked India with the wider world.

sections.title: Mauryan Empire
sections.intro: From Pataliputra the Mauryas ruled India's first great empire. Under Ashoka it turned from conquest to Dhamma, leaving edicts carved in stone across the land.

exhibits.title: Chandragupta Maurya
exhibits.text: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the Nanda king around 321 BCE and founded the Maurya empire, the first to unite most of the subcontinent. He defeated Seleucus Nicator and gained lands in the north-west. By Jain tradition, he ended his life as a monk at Shravanabelagola.
exhibits.show: Chandragiri Hill and Bhadrabahu cave, Shravanabelagola (Jain tradition of Chandragupta's last years)

exhibits.title: Chanakya
exhibits.text: Chanakya, also called Kautilya or Vishnugupta, was Chandragupta's teacher and minister. The Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft, economy and law, is attributed to him, though parts of it may have been written later.
exhibits.show: Arthashastra palm-leaf manuscript (text rediscovered by R. Shamasastry, Mysore, 1905)

exhibits.title: Bindusara
exhibits.text: Bindusara, son of Chandragupta, ruled from about 297 to 273 BCE and extended the empire into the Deccan. Greek sources call him Amitrochates, slayer of foes. He kept diplomatic ties with the Seleucid kingdom of Syria.
exhibits.show: Map of the Maurya empire under Bindusara/Ashoka, c. 260 BCE

exhibits.title: Ashoka
exhibits.text: Ashoka ruled from about 268 to 232 BCE. After the Kalinga war he turned to Buddhism and a policy of Dhamma. His edicts, carved on rocks and pillars across the subcontinent, are the earliest deciphered Indian inscriptions, mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script.
exhibits.show: Kanaganahalli (Sannati) stupa relief inscribed 'Raya Asoko' showing Ashoka with queens

exhibits.title: Kalinga War
exhibits.text: Around 261 BCE Ashoka conquered Kalinga, in present-day Odisha. In his Thirteenth Rock Edict he records that a hundred thousand people were killed and a hundred and fifty thousand deported, and expresses deep remorse. He turned from conquest by war to conquest by Dhamma.
exhibits.show: Dhauli hill: Ashokan rock edict with rock-cut elephant, near Bhubaneswar

exhibits.title: Ashoka's Dhamma
exhibits.text: Ashoka's Dhamma was a moral code: respect for elders, kindness to servants and animals, tolerance of all sects and restraint in speech. He appointed dhamma-mahamattas to spread it and sent missions abroad, including his son Mahinda to Sri Lanka.
exhibits.show: Ashokan pillar at Lauriya Nandangarh (intact lion capital, inscribed Pillar Edicts)

exhibits.title: Mauryan administration
exhibits.text: The empire was ruled from Pataliputra and divided into provinces under princes. A large bureaucracy collected taxes and ran a standing army and a network of spies. Megasthenes, the Greek envoy, described the city councils of Pataliputra in his Indica.
exhibits.show: Kumrahar excavations of Pataliputra (Mauryan pillared hall remains), Patna

exhibits.title: Mauryan economy
exhibits.text: The state controlled mines, forests and many industries, collected land revenue of about a quarter of the produce, and regulated trade, weights and prices. Punch-marked silver coins circulated widely, and roads linked the empire.
exhibits.show: Mauryan punch-marked silver karshapana coin

exhibits.title: Mauryan art and architecture
exhibits.text: Polished sandstone pillars crowned with animal capitals, such as the Lion Capital of Sarnath, now India's national emblem; the rock-cut Barabar caves; early stupas such as Sanchi; and the Didarganj Yakshi show the court art of the age.
exhibits.show: Lomas Rishi Cave entrance, Barabar Hills, Bihar

exhibits.title: Decline of the Mauryas
exhibits.text: After Ashoka the empire weakened under less able successors, financial strain and regional revolts. In about 185 BCE the general Pushyamitra Shunga killed the last Maurya, Brihadratha, and founded the Shunga dynasty.
exhibits.show: Bharhut stupa railing and gateway (Shunga period), Indian Museum Kolkata

quiz.q: Whom did Chandragupta Maurya overthrow to found the Maurya empire?
quiz.why: He overthrew the Nanda king around 321 BCE.

quiz.q: Which war led Ashoka to turn from conquest by war to conquest by Dhamma?
quiz.why: His Thirteenth Rock Edict expresses remorse for the Kalinga war.

quiz.q: Which treatise on statecraft is attributed to Chanakya?
quiz.why: The Arthashastra, on statecraft, economy and law, is attributed to Chanakya (Kautilya).

centre.show: Sarnath Lion Capital of Ashoka, Sarnath Museum

sections.title: Post-Mauryan India
sections.intro: After the Mauryas, rulers from Central Asia and the Deccan created new kingdoms. Trade with Rome and along the Silk Route made this an age of wealth, art and exchange.

exhibits.title: Indo-Greeks
exhibits.text: Greek rulers from Bactria entered north-west India in the 2nd century BCE. The most famous, Menander, or Milinda, discussed philosophy with the monk Nagasena in the Milindapanha. The Indo-Greeks issued fine coins bearing their kings' portraits and names.
exhibits.show: Silver drachm/tetradrachm of Menander I with Greek and Kharoshthi legends

exhibits.title: Shakas
exhibits.text: The Shakas, or Scythians, from Central Asia ruled parts of northern and western India. The Western Kshatrapas held Gujarat and Malwa, and Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription of about 150 CE is an early long inscription in Sanskrit. The Shaka era of 78 CE is used in India's national calendar.
exhibits.show: Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman I (c. 150 CE), Girnar

exhibits.title: Parthians
exhibits.text: The Indo-Parthians, or Pahlavas, ruled the north-west in the 1st century CE. Gondophares is the best known of them; Christian tradition links the apostle Saint Thomas to his court.
exhibits.show: Silver coin of Gondophares (king on horseback), Indo-Parthian

exhibits.title: Kushanas
exhibits.text: The Kushanas, a branch of the Yuezhi of Central Asia, built an empire from Central Asia to the Ganga plain between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE. They issued many gold coins and fostered the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
exhibits.show: Gandhara standing Buddha in grey schist (Kushan period)

exhibits.title: Kanishka
exhibits.text: Kanishka, the greatest Kushana ruler, is usually dated to the late 1st or early 2nd century CE. He patronised Buddhism and convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir, and the poet Ashvaghosha and the physician Charaka are associated with his court.
exhibits.show: Headless statue of Kanishka, Government Museum Mathura

exhibits.title: Satavahanas
exhibits.text: The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan from about the 1st century BCE to the 3rd century CE. Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated the Shakas. They issued lead and potin coins, granted land to Brahmins and Buddhists, and patronised caves at Karla, Nashik and the stupa at Amaravati.
exhibits.show: Great Stupa at Sanchi, north/south gateway (torana) with Satavahana-era inscription

exhibits.title: Trade with Rome
exhibits.text: Trade boomed. Indian pepper, spices, textiles, gems and ivory went to the Roman empire, and Roman gold coins and wine came back. Ports such as Barygaza, now Bharuch, and Muziris thrived, and merchant guilds funded monasteries and caves.
exhibits.show: Roman gold aureus / denarius from South Indian hoards (e.g. Augustus or Tiberius)

exhibits.title: Silk Route
exhibits.text: The Silk Route linked China with the Mediterranean through Central Asia. The Kushanas controlled key sections, and branches ran into India. Along it travelled silk, spices, horses and ideas, including Buddhism, which reached China this way.
exhibits.show: Map of the Silk Road with its branches into the Indian subcontinent, 1st–3rd c. CE

quiz.q: Menander (Milinda) discussed philosophy with which monk in the Milindapanha?
quiz.why: The Milindapanha records Menander's dialogue with Nagasena.

quiz.q: Which Kushana ruler convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir?
quiz.why: Kanishka patronised Buddhism and convened the Fourth Buddhist Council.

quiz.q: The Shaka era used in India's national calendar begins in which year?
quiz.why: The Shaka era of 78 CE is used in the national calendar.

centre.show: Gold dinar of Kanishka I with Buddha ('BODDO') reverse, British Museum

sections.title: Sangam Age
sections.intro: In the far south, the Chera, Chola and Pandya kingdoms flourished, and Tamil poets composed the earliest literature of the region, rich in love, war and the life of the land.

exhibits.title: Sangam literature
exhibits.text: Sangam literature is the earliest Tamil poetry, composed roughly between the 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE, traditionally at assemblies, or sangams, in Madurai. Its poems of love, called akam, and of war and public life, called puram, fill anthologies such as Ettuthokai and Pattuppattu. Tolkappiyam is its grammar.
exhibits.show: Tamil palm-leaf manuscript of a Sangam anthology (as recovered by U. V. Swaminatha Iyer)

exhibits.title: The early Cholas
exhibits.text: The early Cholas ruled the Kaveri delta from Uraiyur and the port of Puhar, also called Kaveripattinam. Karikala Chola is remembered for his victories and for building an embankment on the Kaveri, linked by tradition to the Kallanai dam.
exhibits.show: Kallanai (Grand Anicut) on the Kaveri, traditionally attributed to Karikala Chola

exhibits.title: Cheras
exhibits.text: The Cheras ruled the Malabar coast of Kerala, with their capital at Vanji and ports such as Muziris. Their trade with Rome is recorded in Greek and Roman texts. Senguttuvan is a celebrated Chera king.
exhibits.show: Early Chera square copper coin with bow-and-arrow emblem

exhibits.title: The early Pandyas
exhibits.text: The Pandyas ruled the southern tip of India from Madurai, the seat of the Sangam assemblies. They were known to Megasthenes and controlled the pearl fisheries of the Gulf of Mannar. Nedunjeliyan is a famous Pandya king of the Sangam age.
exhibits.show: Early Pandya square copper coin with fish emblem

exhibits.title: Sangam society
exhibits.text: Sangam poems divide the land into five tinais: hills, forest, farmland, coast and dry land, each with its own way of life and emotions. Warriors, poets, including women such as Avvaiyar, farmers and traders appear, and hero stones honoured those who fell in battle.
exhibits.show: Keeladi excavation site, Sivaganga district, Tamil Nadu

exhibits.title: Sangam economy
exhibits.text: Wet rice farming in the river valleys, cotton weaving, pearl fishing, and the export of pepper, ivory and gems supported the economy. Uraiyur was famous for its fine cotton cloth.
exhibits.show: Carnelian and beryl beads from Kodumanal bead-making site, Erode

exhibits.title: Sangam ports
exhibits.text: Muziris, Korkai, Puhar and Arikamedu traded with Rome, South-East Asia and Sri Lanka. At Arikamedu, near Puducherry, Roman pottery and wine jars have been excavated.
exhibits.show: Roman amphora sherds and rouletted ware from Arikamedu, near Puducherry

exhibits.title: Sangam religion
exhibits.text: Murugan was the most popular deity, along with Mayon, or Vishnu, Vendan, or Indra, and Korravai, a goddess of war. Hero stones were worshipped, and Buddhism, Jainism and Vedic sacrifice also had a place.
exhibits.show: Tamil-Brahmi inscribed hero stone (nadukal), e.g. Pulimankombai

quiz.q: In Sangam poetry, poems of love are called what?
quiz.why: Akam poems deal with love; puram with war and public life.

quiz.q: Which city was the capital of the Pandyas and seat of the Sangam assemblies?
quiz.why: The Pandyas ruled from Madurai, where the sangams were traditionally held.

quiz.q: At which site near Puducherry have Roman pottery and wine jars been excavated?
quiz.why: Excavations at Arikamedu revealed Roman pottery and amphorae.

centre.show: Satavahana lead coin with two-masted ship, as reference for an early Indian Ocean trading vessel

sections.title: Gupta Empire
sections.intro: Under the Guptas, north India saw great achievements in mathematics, astronomy, literature and art, though historians now debate how golden this age really was.

exhibits.title: Chandragupta I
exhibits.text: Chandragupta the First, who ruled from about 319 to 335 CE, raised the Gupta dynasty to power, helped by his marriage to the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi. The Gupta era is counted from 319 to 320 CE.
exhibits.show: Chandragupta I–Kumaradevi gold dinar (king-and-queen type)

exhibits.title: Samudragupta
exhibits.text: Samudragupta, who ruled from about 335 to 375 CE, campaigned across north and south India. His Allahabad Pillar inscription, composed by the poet Harishena, lists his conquests. A musician too, he appears playing the veena on his coins.
exhibits.show: Allahabad (Prayagraj) Pillar with Samudragupta's prashasti

exhibits.title: Chandragupta II
exhibits.text: Chandragupta the Second, also called Vikramaditya, ruled from about 375 to 415 CE. He defeated the Western Shakas, adding Gujarat and Malwa and access to the western ports. The Chinese pilgrim Faxian visited India in his reign, and tradition links the poet Kalidasa to his court.
exhibits.show: Chandragupta II lion-slayer gold dinar

exhibits.title: Gupta administration
exhibits.text: Gupta kings took grand titles such as Maharajadhiraja, king of great kings. Provinces, called bhuktis, and districts, called vishayas, were run by officials; many posts became hereditary, and land grants to Brahmins and officials increased.
exhibits.show: Gupta-period copper-plate land grant with seal ring (e.g. Damodarpur plates)

exhibits.title: Gupta economy
exhibits.text: The Guptas issued the largest number of gold coins of any ancient Indian dynasty, called dinaras. Agriculture, crafts and guilds flourished, though some historians see a decline in long-distance trade with Rome and a rise in land grants.
exhibits.show: Gupta gold dinar, archer type (e.g. Chandragupta II)

exhibits.title: Gupta science
exhibits.text: Aryabhata proposed that the earth rotates on its axis and explained eclipses scientifically. Varahamihira wrote the Brihat Samhita on astronomy and natural science. Metalworkers produced the rust-resistant Iron Pillar that now stands in Delhi.
exhibits.show: Statue of Aryabhata at IUCAA, Pune (modern imaginative likeness)

exhibits.title: Gupta-era mathematics
exhibits.text: The decimal place-value system with zero developed in India in this era. Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya, of 499 CE, gave a value of pi close to 3.1416 and methods in algebra and trigonometry. These ideas later reached Europe through the Arab world.
exhibits.show: Bakhshali manuscript folio showing the dot-zero, Bodleian Library

exhibits.title: Gupta literature
exhibits.text: Sanskrit literature flourished. Kalidasa wrote Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta and Raghuvamsha; Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa; and Shudraka, Mrichchhakatika. The Panchatantra and the later forms of the Puranas belong to this broad period.
exhibits.show: Raja Ravi Varma's 'Shakuntala' painting (public domain)

exhibits.title: Gupta art
exhibits.text: Gupta art set classical standards: the serene Buddha images of Sarnath, the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh, early stone temples, and the paintings of the Ajanta caves, produced largely under the neighbouring Vakatakas.
exhibits.show: Seated Buddha preaching the First Sermon, Sarnath Museum (5th c.)

exhibits.title: Religion in the Gupta age
exhibits.text: Gupta kings were mainly devotees of Vishnu, and Puranic Hinduism with temple worship grew. Buddhism and Jainism also flourished; the great monastery of Nalanda was founded in the 5th century under Kumaragupta.
exhibits.show: Varaha panel, Udayagiri Cave 5, near Vidisha

exhibits.title: A golden age?
exhibits.text: The Gupta period was once called India's golden age for its art, science and literature. Historians now point out that this view overlooks growing caste rigidity, the spread of untouchability, the declining status of women and the growth of land grants.
exhibits.show: Dashavatara Temple, Deogarh – Vishnu Anantashayana panel

exhibits.title: Decline of the Guptas
exhibits.text: From the late 5th century, Huna invasions from Central Asia, weak successors, rising feudatories and falling revenue weakened the empire. By the mid-6th century it had broken into regional kingdoms.
exhibits.show: Eran Varaha boar with Toramana's inscription, Eran, Madhya Pradesh

quiz.q: Who composed the Allahabad Pillar inscription listing Samudragupta's conquests?
quiz.why: The prashasti was composed by the poet Harishena.

quiz.q: Which Chinese pilgrim visited India in the reign of Chandragupta II?
quiz.why: Faxian visited India during Chandragupta II's reign.

quiz.q: In which year was Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya written?
quiz.why: The Aryabhatiya dates to 499 CE.

centre.show: Iron Pillar of Delhi, Qutb complex, Mehrauli

sections.title: Post-Gupta Period
sections.intro: After the Guptas, regional dynasties rose across India, fought over Kannauj, and built magnificent rock-cut and stone temples.

exhibits.title: Harshavardhana
exhibits.text: Harshavardhana ruled much of north India from Kannauj between 606 and 647 CE. Banabhatta wrote his biography, the Harshacharita, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang described his court and the great assembly at Prayag. He was halted on the Narmada by Pulakeshin the Second.
exhibits.show: Banskhera copper plate of Harsha bearing his signature

exhibits.title: Pushyabhutis
exhibits.text: The Pushyabhuti, or Vardhana, dynasty began at Thanesar in Haryana. Prabhakaravardhana resisted the Hunas, and his sons Rajyavardhana and Harshavardhana followed him. Harsha moved the capital to Kannauj, which became the great prize of north Indian politics.
exhibits.show: Harsh ka Tila mound, Thanesar (Kurukshetra)

exhibits.title: Chalukyas of Badami
exhibits.text: The Chalukyas of Badami, or Vatapi, in Karnataka, ruled the Deccan from the 6th to the 8th centuries. Pulakeshin the Second defeated Harsha. Their temples at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal, a UNESCO site, mark a key stage in temple architecture.
exhibits.show: Badami cave temples (Cave 3) above Agastya lake

exhibits.title: Pallavas
exhibits.text: The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram in Tamil Nadu from about the 6th to the 9th centuries. Mahendravarman and Narasimhavarman built the rock-cut monuments of Mamallapuram, including the Shore Temple and the Pancha Rathas. They fought long wars with the Chalukyas.
exhibits.show: Descent of the Ganges (Arjuna's Penance) relief, Mamallapuram

exhibits.title: Rashtrakutas
exhibits.text: The Rashtrakutas of Manyakheta, in Karnataka, were among the strongest powers of the 8th to 10th centuries. Krishna the First built the Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved from a single rock. Amoghavarsha was a noted patron of literature.
exhibits.show: Kailasa Temple (Cave 16), Ellora

exhibits.title: Gurjara-Pratiharas
exhibits.text: The Gurjara-Pratiharas ruled western and northern India from the 8th to the 10th centuries, eventually from Kannauj. Rulers such as Nagabhata the First and Mihira Bhoja resisted Arab expansion from Sindh.
exhibits.show: Batesar temple group, Morena (Gurjara-Pratihara period)

exhibits.title: Palas
exhibits.text: The Palas ruled Bengal and Bihar from the 8th to the 12th centuries. Gopala, their founder, was reportedly chosen by local chiefs. Dharmapala founded the monastery of Vikramashila and supported Nalanda, and Pala art influenced Tibet and South-East Asia.
exhibits.show: Vikramashila Mahavihara ruins, Antichak, Bhagalpur

exhibits.title: Rise of regional kingdoms
exhibits.text: After the Guptas, power shifted to regional kingdoms. The long contest among the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas for Kannauj is called the tripartite struggle. Regional languages, scripts and temple styles grew alongside these states.
exhibits.show: Map of the tripartite struggle for Kannauj, c. 800 CE (Palas, Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas)

quiz.q: Which king halted Harshavardhana on the Narmada?
quiz.why: Harsha was stopped on the Narmada by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II.

quiz.q: Which Rashtrakuta king built the Kailasa temple at Ellora?
quiz.why: Krishna I had the Kailasa temple carved from a single rock.

quiz.q: The tripartite struggle was fought over control of which city?
quiz.why: Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas contested Kannauj.

centre.show: Pancha Rathas, Mamallapuram – Dharmaraja Ratha

wings.title: Medieval India
wings.subtitle: Rajputs, Sultans, saints and Mughals
wings.intro: Welcome to Medieval India: temple builders and Rajput kings, the sultans of Delhi, the poet-saints of bhakti and Sufism, the Mughal empire and the regional powers that followed.

sections.title: Early Medieval India
sections.intro: Rajput kingdoms, great temples and the first waves of devotional poetry shaped the early medieval centuries, as regional states and identities took root.

exhibits.title: Rajputs
exhibits.text: From the 8th century, Rajput clans such as the Chauhans, Paramaras, Chandelas, Gahadavalas and Solankis ruled much of northern and western India. Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Muhammad of Ghor at Tarain in 1191, but lost to him there in 1192.
exhibits.show: Bull-and-horseman coin of Prithviraj III Chauhan

exhibits.title: Temple architecture
exhibits.text: Temple styles matured: the Nagara style of the north, with curved towers, as at Khajuraho and Konark; the Dravida style of the south, with pyramidal towers and gateway gopurams; and the Vesara style of the Deccan, which blends the two.
exhibits.show: Chariot wheel of the Sun Temple, Konark

exhibits.title: Early bhakti
exhibits.text: Bhakti, loving devotion to a personal god, began among the Tamil Alvars and Nayanars between the 6th and 9th centuries. They sang in Tamil rather than Sanskrit and welcomed devotees of every caste.
exhibits.show: Chola bronze of Saint Manikkavachakar

exhibits.title: Regional states
exhibits.text: Kingdoms such as those of Kashmir, described in Kalhana's Rajatarangini, the Eastern Gangas of Odisha, the Kalachuris and the Kakatiyas built regional identities through language, temples and land grants.
exhibits.show: Martand Sun Temple ruins, Kashmir (Karkota, 8th c.)

exhibits.title: Early medieval trade
exhibits.text: Some historians see a decline in coinage and long-distance trade in the early medieval north, while others stress its continuity. Arab merchants were active on the west coast, and South Indian guilds such as the Ainnurruvar traded overseas.
exhibits.show: Bull-and-horseman jital of the Hindu Shahis

exhibits.title: Early medieval society
exhibits.text: Castes, or jatis, multiplied as tribes and occupational groups were absorbed into society; land grants created a landed class; and Rajput codes of honour shaped elite values.
exhibits.show: Leiden copper plates (Chola land grant, 11th c.)

quiz.q: Where did Prithviraj Chauhan defeat Muhammad of Ghor in 1191?
quiz.why: Prithviraj won the first battle of Tarain in 1191 but lost there in 1192.

quiz.q: Which temple style, with curved towers, is found at Khajuraho and Konark?
quiz.why: The northern Nagara style is known for its curved towers.

quiz.q: In which language did the Alvars and Nayanars sing their devotional hymns?
quiz.why: They sang in Tamil rather than Sanskrit, reaching devotees of every caste.

centre.show: Kandariya Mahadeva temple, Khajuraho (Nagara shikhara)

sections.title: South Indian Kingdoms
sections.intro: Chola admirals, Hoysala sculptors, Kakatiya builders and the rulers of Vijayanagara made the south a centre of power, trade and art.

exhibits.title: Imperial Cholas
exhibits.text: Founded by Vijayalaya in the 9th century, the Chola empire peaked under Rajaraja the First and Rajendra the First. They built the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur, sent naval expeditions to Sri Lanka and South-East Asia, and are famed for village assemblies and bronze sculpture.
exhibits.show: Brihadishvara temple vimana, Thanjavur

exhibits.title: Hoysalas
exhibits.text: The Hoysalas ruled southern Karnataka from the 11th to the 14th centuries, from Dvarasamudra, now Halebidu. Their star-shaped temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura, richly carved in soapstone, are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
exhibits.show: Hoysaleswara temple, Halebidu (stellate carved walls)

exhibits.title: Kakatiyas
exhibits.text: The Kakatiyas ruled Telangana and Andhra from Warangal in the 12th to 14th centuries. Rudramadevi was one of India's few reigning queens. The Ramappa temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and their lake tanks supported farming.
exhibits.show: Kakatiya Kala Thoranam (stone gateway), Warangal Fort

exhibits.title: The later Pandyas
exhibits.text: The Pandyas revived in the 13th century and briefly dominated the south; Marco Polo visited their coast. Malik Kafur's raid in 1311 and civil wars weakened them, and the short-lived Madurai Sultanate followed.
exhibits.show: Pandya coin with double-fish emblem

exhibits.title: Vijayanagara Empire
exhibits.text: Founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka, the Vijayanagara empire dominated the south for over two centuries. Krishnadevaraya was its greatest ruler. After the battle of Talikota in 1565 its capital, Hampi, was sacked; its ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
exhibits.show: Stone Chariot, Vittala temple, Hampi

exhibits.title: Bahmani Sultanate
exhibits.text: The Bahmani Sultanate was founded in 1347 by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah in the Deccan, with capitals at Gulbarga and Bidar. The minister Mahmud Gawan reformed its administration. It later split into five Deccan sultanates, including Bijapur and Golconda.
exhibits.show: Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan, Bidar

quiz.q: Which dynasty built the Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur?
quiz.why: The Imperial Cholas built the Brihadishvara temple and sent naval expeditions overseas.

quiz.q: Who founded the Vijayanagara empire in 1336?
quiz.why: Vijayanagara was founded by the brothers Harihara and Bukka in 1336.

quiz.q: Which famous queen ruled the Kakatiya kingdom from Warangal?
quiz.why: Rudramadevi was one of India's few reigning queens.

centre.show: Chola bronze Nataraja (Shiva as Lord of Dance)

sections.title: Delhi Sultanate
sections.intro: Five dynasties ruled from Delhi for over three centuries, introducing new forms of government, architecture and culture.

exhibits.title: The Mamluk or Slave dynasty
exhibits.text: The Mamluk, or Slave, dynasty, from 1206 to 1290, was founded by Qutbuddin Aibak. Iltutmish consolidated the sultanate and introduced the silver tanka; Razia was the only woman to rule as sultan of Delhi; and Balban strengthened royal power.
exhibits.show: Silver tanka of Iltutmish

exhibits.title: Khalji Dynasty
exhibits.text: The Khaljis, from 1290 to 1320, were led by Alauddin Khalji, who repelled Mongol invasions, sent his general Malik Kafur on raids deep into the south, and introduced market controls and land revenue based on measured land.
exhibits.show: Alai Darwaza, Qutb complex, Delhi

exhibits.title: Tughlaq Dynasty
exhibits.text: The Tughlaqs, from 1320 to 1414, included Muhammad bin Tughlaq, known for bold but failed experiments such as shifting the capital to Daulatabad and a token currency, and Firoz Shah Tughlaq, who built canals and towns. Timur sacked Delhi in 1398.
exhibits.show: Brass/copper token coin of Muhammad bin Tughlaq

exhibits.title: Sayyid Dynasty
exhibits.text: The Sayyids, from 1414 to 1451, were founded by Khizr Khan, who had served as Timur's governor. Their power was limited to the area around Delhi.
exhibits.show: Tomb of Muhammad Shah Sayyid, Lodhi Garden, Delhi

exhibits.title: Lodi Dynasty
exhibits.text: The Lodis, Afghan rulers from 1451 to 1526, included Bahlul, Sikandar, who founded the city of Agra, and Ibrahim Lodi, who was defeated and killed by Babur at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526, ending the sultanate.
exhibits.show: Tomb of Sikandar Lodi, Lodhi Garden, Delhi

exhibits.title: Sultanate administration
exhibits.text: The sultan was the supreme ruler, helped by ministers such as the wazir. Land was assigned as iqtas to officers, who collected revenue and maintained troops. Persian was the language of administration.
exhibits.show: Map of the Delhi Sultanate at its greatest extent (c. 1335)

exhibits.title: Sultanate economy
exhibits.text: Land revenue was the main source of income. Towns and crafts grew, along with trade with Central and West Asia. The Persian wheel and the spinning wheel spread, and the silver tanka and copper jital became standard coins.
exhibits.show: Persian wheel (rahat) lifting water from a well

exhibits.title: Sultanate military
exhibits.text: The sultans kept a large standing army of cavalry, with horses imported from Central Asia and Arabia, and war elephants. Alauddin Khalji introduced the branding of horses, called dagh, and descriptive rolls of soldiers, called huliya.
exhibits.show: Walls and bastions of Tughlaqabad Fort, Delhi

exhibits.title: Sultanate architecture
exhibits.text: Indo-Islamic architecture introduced the true arch and dome: the Qutub Minar and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, the Alai Darwaza, Tughlaqabad fort and the Lodi tombs. The Qutub complex is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
exhibits.show: Tomb of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Tughlaqabad

exhibits.title: Sultanate society
exhibits.text: Society included Turkish, Afghan and Indian nobles, religious scholars, merchants, artisans and peasants. Persian culture met Indian traditions, giving rise to new music, poetry and the Hindavi language, as in the work of Amir Khusrau.
exhibits.show: Amir Khusrau with disciples (later Mughal miniature)

quiz.q: Who founded the Mamluk, or Slave, dynasty in 1206?
quiz.why: Qutbuddin Aibak founded the dynasty; Iltutmish later consolidated it.

quiz.q: Which Tughlaq sultan shifted the capital to Daulatabad and issued a token currency?
quiz.why: Muhammad bin Tughlaq is known for these bold but failed experiments.

quiz.q: What were the land assignments given to officers to collect revenue and maintain troops called?
quiz.why: Under the Sultanate, land was assigned to officers as iqtas.

centre.show: Qutb Minar, Delhi

sections.title: Bhakti and Sufi Movements
sections.intro: Saints and mystics taught that love of God matters more than ritual or birth, and sang their message in the languages of the people.

exhibits.title: Bhakti saints
exhibits.text: Bhakti saints taught that sincere devotion matters more than ritual or caste. Across regions they sang in local languages: Basavanna in Kannada; Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram in Marathi; Tulsidas and Surdas in Hindi; and many more.
exhibits.show: Vitthal (Vithoba) temple, Pandharpur

exhibits.title: Alvars
exhibits.text: The twelve Alvars were Tamil poet-saints devoted to Vishnu, active between about the 6th and 9th centuries. Their hymns are collected in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham, and Andal is the only woman among them.
exhibits.show: Bronze of Andal, the woman Alvar saint

exhibits.title: Nayanars
exhibits.text: The sixty-three Nayanars were Tamil saints devoted to Shiva. Their hymns form the Tevaram. Saints such as Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar came from different castes, and Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a woman saint.
exhibits.show: Chola bronze of child-saint Sambandar dancing

exhibits.title: Kabir
exhibits.text: Kabir, a 15th-century weaver of Varanasi, rejected ritual and caste in both Hinduism and Islam and praised a formless God. His sharp couplets, or dohas, are in everyday Hindi, and some appear in the Guru Granth Sahib.
exhibits.show: Kabir weaving at his loom (Mughal/Company-era painting)

exhibits.title: Guru Nanak
exhibits.text: Guru Nanak, born in 1469 at Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib, founded Sikhism. He taught devotion to one God, honest work, sharing and equality, began the langar, the community kitchen, and travelled widely to spread his message. He died in 1539.
exhibits.show: Janamsakhi illustration of Guru Nanak

exhibits.title: Mirabai
exhibits.text: Mirabai, a 16th-century Rajput princess, devoted herself to Krishna, defying royal and social expectations. Her songs in Rajasthani and Braj are still sung across India.
exhibits.show: Rajasthani miniature of Mirabai singing to Krishna

exhibits.title: Chaitanya
exhibits.text: Chaitanya Mahaprabhu of Bengal, who lived from 1486 to 1534, led ecstatic devotion to Krishna through kirtan, group singing and dancing. His followers founded Gaudiya Vaishnavism, which later inspired the ISKCON movement.
exhibits.show: Painting of Chaitanya leading sankirtan

exhibits.title: Sufi orders
exhibits.text: Sufism, the mystical path in Islam, reached India with orders, or silsilas, such as the Chishti, Suhrawardi, Qadiri and Naqshbandi. Chishti saints like Moinuddin Chishti of Ajmer and Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi welcomed people of every background.
exhibits.show: Dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya, Delhi

exhibits.title: Impact of Bhakti and Sufism
exhibits.text: Bhakti and Sufi movements enriched regional languages and music, including qawwali and kirtan, challenged caste barriers, and encouraged dialogue between Hindu and Muslim traditions. Their shrines and songs remain living traditions.
exhibits.show: Mughal painting of Sufis in sama (dancing dervishes)

quiz.q: Who is the only woman among the twelve Alvars?
quiz.why: Andal is the only woman among the Alvars; Karaikkal Ammaiyar was a Nayanar.

quiz.q: Which practice did Guru Nanak begin?
quiz.why: Guru Nanak began the langar, a community kitchen open to all.

quiz.q: Which Sufi order did Moinuddin Chishti of Ajmer and Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi belong to?
quiz.why: Both were saints of the Chishti silsila.

centre.show: Saraswati veena (South Indian veena)

sections.title: Mughal Empire
sections.intro: From Babur to Aurangzeb, the Mughals built one of the world's largest and richest empires, famous for its administration, gardens, paintings and monuments.

exhibits.title: Babur
exhibits.text: Babur, a Timurid prince from Fergana, defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526 using field guns and cavalry tactics, founding the Mughal empire. He then defeated Rana Sanga at Khanwa in 1527. His memoir, the Baburnama, describes India vividly.
exhibits.show: Babur laying out the Garden of Fidelity, Baburnama folio

exhibits.title: Humayun
exhibits.text: Humayun lost his kingdom to Sher Shah Suri in 1540 and spent fifteen years in exile, partly in Persia. He regained Delhi in 1555 but died the following year. His garden tomb in Delhi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
exhibits.show: Humayun's Tomb, Delhi

exhibits.title: Sher Shah Suri
exhibits.text: Sher Shah Suri, who ruled from 1540 to 1545, built an efficient administration: land measurement, the silver rupiya coin, roadside inns called sarais, and the highway later known as the Grand Trunk Road. Akbar adopted many of his reforms.
exhibits.show: Silver rupiya of Sher Shah Suri

exhibits.title: Akbar
exhibits.text: Akbar, who ruled from 1556 to 1605, expanded the empire across north India and into the Deccan, built alliances with Rajput rulers, abolished the jizya tax and encouraged debate among faiths at Fatehpur Sikri. His policy of sulh-i-kul, peace with all, shaped Mughal rule.
exhibits.show: Akbarnama folio showing Akbar (V&A Akbarnama paintings)

exhibits.title: Jahangir
exhibits.text: Jahangir, who ruled from 1605 to 1627, loved art and nature, and painting flourished under him. His wife Nur Jahan held great influence. He received the English envoy Sir Thomas Roe, and is remembered for his chain of justice.
exhibits.show: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings, by Bichitr (Freer Gallery)

exhibits.title: Shah Jahan
exhibits.text: Shah Jahan, who ruled from 1628 to 1658, presided over the empire's grandest building: the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and the Jama Masjid of Delhi, and the Peacock Throne. He was deposed by his son Aurangzeb and died a captive in Agra.
exhibits.show: Shah Jahan on Horseback, Shah Jahan Album (The Met)

exhibits.title: Aurangzeb
exhibits.text: Aurangzeb, who ruled from 1658 to 1707, expanded the empire to its greatest size, including the Deccan sultanates. Long wars against the Marathas, revolts, the reimposition of jizya and his orthodox policies strained the empire.
exhibits.show: Contemporary Mughal portrait of Aurangzeb

exhibits.title: Mughal administration
exhibits.text: The emperor ruled through ministers such as the wakil, diwan, mir bakhshi and sadr. The empire was divided into provinces called subas, then sarkars and parganas, with Persian as the language of government.
exhibits.show: Map of Mughal subas under Akbar (c. 1605)

exhibits.title: Mansabdari system
exhibits.text: Akbar's mansabdari system ranked every officer by zat, personal rank, and sawar, the number of cavalry to be maintained. Mansabdars were usually paid through jagirs, assignments of land revenue that were transferred to prevent local power bases.
exhibits.show: Padshahnama durbar scene with nobles ranked in rows

exhibits.title: Mughal revenue system
exhibits.text: Under Raja Todar Mal, Akbar's revenue system, called zabt or dahsala, assessed land tax from measured land and average yields and prices over ten years. Revenue was usually about a third of the produce, collected in cash.
exhibits.show: Ain-i-Akbari manuscript folio

exhibits.title: Religion under the Mughals
exhibits.text: Akbar held debates in the Ibadat Khana and promoted tolerance; the Din-i-Ilahi was a small spiritual circle around him. Later emperors differed, and Aurangzeb followed a stricter orthodoxy. Many Mughals patronised shrines of several faiths.
exhibits.show: Akbar presiding over debates in the Ibadat Khana (Akbarnama, c. 1605)

exhibits.title: Mughal architecture
exhibits.text: Mughal architecture blended Persian, Central Asian and Indian styles: Humayun's Tomb, Fatehpur Sikri, the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and the four-part charbagh gardens. Its domes, arches, inlay work, red sandstone and marble are famous worldwide.
exhibits.show: Panch Mahal and Buland Darwaza, Fatehpur Sikri

exhibits.title: Mughal literature
exhibits.text: Persian literature thrived: Abul Fazl's Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari, Persian translations of the Mahabharata and Ramayana, and Dara Shikoh's work on the Upanishads. Tulsidas wrote the Ramcharitmanas during Akbar's reign.
exhibits.show: Razmnama (Persian Mahabharata) illustrated folio

exhibits.title: Mughal economy
exhibits.text: The Mughal empire was among the largest economies in the world, exporting textiles, indigo and spices. The silver rupee, bankers called sarrafs with bills of exchange called hundis, and cities such as Agra, Lahore and Surat flourished.
exhibits.show: Silver rupee of Akbar

exhibits.title: Decline of the Mughals
exhibits.text: After 1707, wars of succession, a crisis in the jagir system, rising regional powers such as the Marathas and Sikhs, and invasions by Nadir Shah in 1739 and Ahmad Shah Abdali weakened the empire. By 1803 the emperor was under British protection.
exhibits.show: Bahadur Shah Zafar photographed in 1858 (last Mughal emperor)

quiz.q: Whom did Babur defeat at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526?
quiz.why: Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat, founding the Mughal empire.

quiz.q: Which ruler introduced the silver rupiya and built sarais along the highway later called the Grand Trunk Road?
quiz.why: Sher Shah Suri introduced these reforms during his rule from 1540 to 1545.

quiz.q: In the mansabdari system, what did the sawar rank indicate?
options: Number of cavalry to be maintained
quiz.why: Zat was the personal rank; sawar was the number of cavalry to be kept.

centre.show: Taj Mahal, Agra

sections.title: Regional Powers
sections.intro: As Mughal power declined, new regional states rose across India, from the Marathas and Sikhs to Mysore, Awadh, Hyderabad and Bengal.

exhibits.title: Marathas
exhibits.text: The Marathas rose in the Deccan in the 17th century, building on hill forts and mobile cavalry. After Shivaji, they resisted Aurangzeb, and in the 18th century became the leading power in India.
exhibits.show: Map of the Maratha confederacy c. 1758

exhibits.title: Shivaji
exhibits.text: Shivaji, who lived from 1630 to 1680, carved out an independent kingdom from Bijapur and Mughal territory, built forts and a navy, and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674. He ruled with a council of eight ministers, the Ashta Pradhan.
exhibits.show: Late-17th-century portrait of Shivaji (Deccani style)

exhibits.title: Peshwas
exhibits.text: From Balaji Vishwanath in 1713, the Peshwas, or chief ministers, led the Maratha state from Pune. Baji Rao the First expanded Maratha power north, and the Marathas reached Delhi and Attock, but suffered a heavy defeat by Ahmad Shah Abdali at Panipat in 1761.
exhibits.show: Shaniwar Wada gateway, Pune

exhibits.title: Sikhs
exhibits.text: After Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa in 1699, Sikh groups called misls rose in Punjab. Maharaja Ranjit Singh united them and ruled a strong kingdom from Lahore from 1799 to 1839, with a modern army.
exhibits.show: Maharaja Ranjit Singh's golden throne (V&A)

exhibits.title: Mysore
exhibits.text: The kingdom of Mysore became a major power in the 18th century when Haidar Ali took control from the Wodeyar rulers. Mysore modernised its army and resisted British expansion in four wars.
exhibits.show: Daria Daulat Bagh, Srirangapatna

exhibits.title: Haidar Ali
exhibits.text: Haidar Ali, a soldier who rose to command Mysore's army, became its effective ruler from 1761. He built a modern army with European help and defeated the British in the First Anglo-Mysore War, from 1767 to 1769.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Haidar Ali

exhibits.title: Tipu Sultan
exhibits.text: Tipu Sultan, Haidar's son, ruled from 1782 to 1799. He used iron-cased rockets in war, introduced new coins, a new calendar and trade policies, and sought French help. He died defending Srirangapatna in the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War.
exhibits.show: Tipu's Tiger automaton (V&A)

exhibits.title: Awadh
exhibits.text: Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk founded the autonomous state of Awadh in 1722. Its nawabs, ruling from Faizabad and later Lucknow, patronised music, poetry and cuisine. The British annexed Awadh in 1856.
exhibits.show: Bara Imambara, Lucknow

exhibits.title: Hyderabad under the Nizams
exhibits.text: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah founded the state of Hyderabad in 1724 as Mughal governor of the Deccan. The Nizams became allies of the British and ruled until 1948, when Hyderabad joined India.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I

exhibits.title: Bengal Nawabs
exhibits.text: Murshid Quli Khan made Bengal virtually independent; Alivardi Khan and Siraj-ud-Daula followed him. Siraj's defeat at Plassey in 1757 opened the way to British control.
exhibits.show: Robert Clive and Mir Jafar after Plassey, by Francis Hayman (c. 1760)

exhibits.title: Jats
exhibits.text: The Jats, peasant-warriors of the region around Delhi and Agra, built a powerful state under Churaman and Badan Singh. It peaked under Suraj Mal, who died in 1763 and built the fort-palaces of Bharatpur and Deeg.
exhibits.show: Deeg Palace and gardens, Bharatpur

exhibits.title: Rohillas
