exhibits.text: Afghan Rohillas settled in Rohilkhand, in western Uttar Pradesh, in the 18th century under leaders such as Ali Muhammad Khan and Hafiz Rahmat Khan. They were defeated by Awadh with British help in 1774.
exhibits.show: Tomb of Hafiz Rahmat Khan, Bareilly

quiz.q: Where was Shivaji crowned Chhatrapati in 1674?
quiz.why: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674.

quiz.q: Who united the Sikh misls and ruled a kingdom from Lahore from 1799 to 1839?
quiz.why: Ranjit Singh united the misls and ruled from Lahore.

quiz.q: Which Bengal nawab was defeated at Plassey in 1757?
quiz.why: Siraj-ud-Daula's defeat at Plassey opened the way to British control.

centre.show: Maratha hill-fort gateway and bastions (Raigad Fort)

wings.title: Colonial India
wings.subtitle: Europeans, the Company and the Raj
wings.intro: Welcome to Colonial India: how European traders became rulers, how the Company governed, the great revolt of 1857, the reformers who remade society, and the economy under British rule.

sections.title: Arrival of Europeans
sections.intro: European trading companies arrived by sea in search of spices and textiles, built fortified factories, and soon became players in Indian politics.

exhibits.title: Portuguese
exhibits.text: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498, sailing round Africa. Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa in 1510. The Portuguese controlled sea lanes through a system of passes called cartaz, and held Goa until 1961.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Vasco da Gama (16th-c. Portuguese portrait, Lisbon) or Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa

exhibits.title: Dutch
exhibits.text: The Dutch East India Company, founded in 1602, set up trading posts at Masulipatnam, Pulicat and Chinsura and traded in spices and textiles. Defeated by the English at Bedara in 1759, they turned their focus to Indonesia.
exhibits.show: The VOC trading post at Hugli-Chinsura, Bengal, painting by Hendrik van Schuylenburgh (1665, Rijksmuseum)

exhibits.title: Danish
exhibits.text: The Danish East India Company established Tranquebar, now Tharangambadi, in 1620, and later Serampore in Bengal. Missionaries at Serampore pioneered printing in Indian languages. Denmark sold its Indian settlements to Britain in 1845.
exhibits.show: Fort Dansborg, Tharangambadi (Tranquebar), built 1620

exhibits.title: French
exhibits.text: The French East India Company, founded in 1664, was based at Pondicherry. Governor Dupleix built alliances with Indian rulers, but the French lost the Carnatic Wars to Britain, notably at Wandiwash in 1760. Pondicherry joined India in 1954.
exhibits.show: Statue / portrait of Joseph-François Dupleix, Governor of Pondicherry

exhibits.title: British
exhibits.text: The English East India Company received its charter in 1600. Its first factory in India was at Surat, in 1613. It later founded Madras in 1639, acquired Bombay in 1668 and founded Calcutta in 1690, its three presidencies.
exhibits.show: Fort St George on the Coromandel Coast, painting by Jan Van Ryne (1754)

exhibits.title: European trading companies
exhibits.text: European trading companies were joint-stock ventures backed by their governments, with the power to trade, keep armies and make treaties. They bought Indian cotton textiles, indigo, saltpetre and spices, paying largely in silver.
exhibits.show: Coromandel Coast chintz palampore made for the European export market (18th c.)

exhibits.title: Factories: fortified trading posts
exhibits.text: A factory was a fortified trading post where company agents, called factors, lived and stored and bought goods. Fort St George in Madras and Fort William in Calcutta began this way.
exhibits.show: Fort William, Calcutta, painting by George Lambert and Samuel Scott (c.1731)

exhibits.title: European rivalry
exhibits.text: European companies fought one another and joined Indian politics. The Anglo-French Carnatic Wars, from 1746 to 1763, showed that small European-trained armies could decide Indian successions, a lesson the British used to expand their power.
exhibits.show: Plan of the siege of Pondicherry (1748 or 1761) / map of the Carnatic Wars

quiz.q: Which port did Vasco da Gama reach in 1498?
quiz.why: Vasco da Gama sailed round Africa and reached Calicut in 1498.

quiz.q: Where was the English East India Company's first factory in India, set up in 1613?
quiz.why: The Company's first Indian factory was at Surat in 1613.

quiz.q: At which battle in 1760 did the French lose decisively to the British in the Carnatic Wars?
quiz.why: The French lost the Carnatic Wars to Britain, notably at Wandiwash in 1760.

centre.show: 16th-century Portuguese nau (carrack) of the kind Vasco da Gama sailed to Calicut, e.g. São Gabriel (1497)

sections.title: British Expansion
sections.intro: Through battles, treaties and annexations, the East India Company grew from a trading company into the ruler of most of India.

exhibits.title: Battle of Plassey
exhibits.text: On 23 June 1757 Robert Clive defeated Siraj-ud-Daula at Plassey in Bengal, helped by the betrayal of Mir Jafar, who was made Nawab. The battle marked the beginning of British political power in India.
exhibits.show: Robert Clive meeting Mir Jafar after the Battle of Plassey, Francis Hayman painting (c.1760)

exhibits.title: Battle of Buxar
exhibits.text: In 1764 the Company defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and the Mughal emperor Shah Alam the Second at Buxar. The Treaty of Allahabad in 1765 gave the Company the diwani, the right to collect revenue, of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
exhibits.show: Shah Alam II conveying the grant of the Diwani to Robert Clive, Benjamin West (1818) – Treaty of Allahabad 1765

exhibits.title: Subsidiary Alliance
exhibits.text: Under Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance, from 1798, Indian rulers had to keep British troops at their own cost, accept a British resident and not deal with other powers. Hyderabad was the first state to accept it.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Richard Wellesley, Marquess Wellesley, Governor-General 1798–1805

exhibits.title: Doctrine of Lapse
exhibits.text: Under Lord Dalhousie, from 1848 to 1856, a dependent state whose ruler died without a natural heir would lapse to the British; adopted sons were not recognised. Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur were annexed this way.
exhibits.show: Map of India showing states annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse (Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur, etc., 1848–56)

exhibits.title: Anglo-Mysore Wars
exhibits.text: Four wars between 1767 and 1799 between the Company and Mysore, under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan, ended with Tipu's death at Srirangapatna in 1799 and the restoration of the Wodeyars under British control.
exhibits.show: Tipu's Tiger, mechanical organ (Mysore, c.1790s), Victoria and Albert Museum

exhibits.title: Anglo-Maratha Wars
exhibits.text: Three wars between 1775 and 1818 broke Maratha power. The Treaty of Bassein in 1802 made the Peshwa a subsidiary ally, and the third war ended with the Peshwa pensioned off and Maratha territories annexed.
exhibits.show: Shaniwar Wada, Pune – the Peshwas' palace fort, Delhi Darwaza gate

exhibits.title: Anglo-Sikh Wars
exhibits.text: After Ranjit Singh's death, two wars, in 1845 to 1846 and 1848 to 1849, led to the annexation of Punjab in 1849. The Koh-i-Noor diamond was taken from the young Maharaja Duleep Singh.
exhibits.show: Koh-i-Noor diamond (as recut 1852) or Maharaja Duleep Singh, portrait by Franz Xaver Winterhalter (1854)

quiz.q: Who defeated Siraj-ud-Daula at the Battle of Plassey in 1757?
quiz.why: Robert Clive won at Plassey, helped by Mir Jafar's betrayal.

quiz.q: Which state was the first to accept Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance?
quiz.why: Hyderabad was the first state to accept the Subsidiary Alliance.

quiz.q: What did the Treaty of Allahabad (1765) give the Company in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa?
options: The diwani, the right to collect revenue
quiz.why: After Buxar, the treaty granted the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

centre.show: 18th-century Indian bronze cannon, e.g. a Tipu Sultan tiger-headed bronze gun from Mysore

sections.title: East India Company Rule
sections.intro: To govern and profit from its new territories, the Company built systems of revenue, courts, police and education whose effects lasted long after it.

exhibits.title: Company administration
exhibits.text: Company rule developed under governors-general such as Warren Hastings, Cornwallis and Dalhousie, overseen by the British Parliament. A civil service of covenanted officers ran districts through collectors.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Warren Hastings by Tilly Kettle or Joshua Reynolds

exhibits.title: Land revenue systems
exhibits.text: To fund itself, the Company experimented with land revenue settlements that fixed who paid tax and how much. Three main systems emerged in different regions: the Permanent Settlement, Ryotwari and Mahalwari.
exhibits.show: Company School painting of Indian cultivators ploughing / revenue officials at work (c.1800–1850)

exhibits.title: Permanent Settlement
exhibits.text: Introduced by Cornwallis in 1793 in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, the Permanent Settlement made zamindars owners of the land, with revenue fixed forever. It ensured a steady income but left peasants at the mercy of zamindars.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Charles, 1st Marquess Cornwallis (Thomas Gainsborough, 1783)

exhibits.title: Ryotwari system
exhibits.text: Introduced by Thomas Munro and Alexander Read in Madras and later in Bombay, the Ryotwari system collected revenue directly from cultivators, or ryots, with periodic reassessment, often at high rates.
exhibits.show: Equestrian statue of Sir Thomas Munro, Chennai (Francis Chantrey, 1839)

exhibits.title: Mahalwari system
exhibits.text: Introduced by Holt Mackenzie in 1822 in the North-Western Provinces and later Punjab, the Mahalwari system assessed revenue on a village or estate, called a mahal, as a whole, collected through village headmen.
exhibits.show: Company School painting of a North Indian village with headman and accountant (patwari)

exhibits.title: Courts and law
exhibits.text: Warren Hastings set up civil and criminal courts in districts, and Cornwallis separated judicial and revenue work. The Supreme Court at Calcutta, in 1774, and later the High Courts, in 1862, applied codified laws such as the Indian Penal Code of 1860.
exhibits.show: The Old Court House, Calcutta, aquatint by Thomas Daniell (Views of Calcutta, 1786–88)

exhibits.title: Colonial police
exhibits.text: Cornwallis created a district police system under officers called daroghas. After 1857 the Police Act of 1861 created a centralised police force, a framework that still shapes policing in India.
exhibits.show: Historic photograph of Indian police constables in uniform (c.1870–1900)

exhibits.title: Colonial education
exhibits.text: Macaulay's Minute of 1835 made English the medium of higher education. Wood's Despatch of 1854 outlined a system from primary schools to universities, and universities opened at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Thomas Babington Macaulay (Minute on Education, 1835) or University of Calcutta (founded 1857)

exhibits.title: Company economic policies
exhibits.text: Free entry for British manufactures, heavy land taxes and a shift to export crops served British industry. India became a supplier of raw materials and a market for British goods.
exhibits.show: Lancashire cotton cloth trade labels ('ticket'/'chop' labels) printed for the Indian market

exhibits.title: Drain of Wealth
exhibits.text: Dadabhai Naoroji, in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, argued that much of India's wealth was drained to Britain through home charges, salaries, pensions and profits, without equal return.
exhibits.show: Photograph of Dadabhai Naoroji and title page of 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901)

quiz.q: Who introduced the Permanent Settlement in Bengal in 1793?
quiz.why: Cornwallis introduced the Permanent Settlement in 1793.

quiz.q: Under the Ryotwari system, revenue was collected directly from whom?
quiz.why: Ryotwari collected revenue directly from the cultivators, or ryots.

quiz.q: Who argued in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' that India's wealth was being drained to Britain?
quiz.why: Dadabhai Naoroji set out the Drain of Wealth theory in that book.

centre.show: East India Company leather-bound account ledger (India Office Records)

sections.title: Revolt of 1857
sections.intro: A great uprising of soldiers, rulers and peasants shook British rule across north and central India and ended the rule of the East India Company.

exhibits.title: Causes of the revolt
exhibits.text: Annexations, heavy revenue demands, the loss of status of rulers and landlords, fears of religious interference and the grievances of sepoys combined. The immediate spark was the new Enfield rifle cartridge, rumoured to be greased with cow and pig fat.
exhibits.show: Paper cartridge for the Enfield rifle (the 'greased cartridge')

exhibits.title: Centres of the revolt
exhibits.text: The revolt began at Meerut on 10 May 1857 and spread to Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Bareilly, Arrah and parts of central India. Punjab, eastern Bengal and most of the south remained largely quiet.
exhibits.show: Map of the main centres of the Revolt of 1857

exhibits.title: Leaders of 1857
exhibits.text: Bahadur Shah Zafar was proclaimed emperor at Delhi. Other leaders included Rani Lakshmibai of Jhansi, Nana Saheb and Tantia Tope at Kanpur, Begum Hazrat Mahal at Lucknow, Kunwar Singh in Bihar and Maulvi Ahmadullah of Faizabad.
exhibits.show: Photograph of Bahadur Shah Zafar in exile awaiting trial, 1858 (attributed to Robert Tytler)

exhibits.title: Course of the revolt
exhibits.text: The British retook Delhi in September 1857 and Lucknow after a long siege. Rani Lakshmibai died fighting near Gwalior in June 1858. By 1859 the revolt had been suppressed with great severity.
exhibits.show: The ruined Residency at Lucknow, photograph by Felice Beato (1858)

exhibits.title: Consequences of the revolt
exhibits.text: The Government of India Act of 1858 ended Company rule, and India came under the British Crown, with a Viceroy. The army was reorganised, annexations stopped, and Queen Victoria's Proclamation promised respect for princes and religions.
exhibits.show: Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1 November 1858

exhibits.title: How 1857 has been understood
exhibits.text: British writers called it the Sepoy Mutiny. V. D. Savarkar, in 1909, called it the First War of Independence. Historians such as S. N. Sen and R. C. Majumdar debated its nature, and recent studies highlight the part played by peasants and ordinary people.
exhibits.show: Title page of V. D. Savarkar's 'The Indian War of Independence of 1857' (1909)

quiz.q: Where did the Revolt of 1857 begin on 10 May 1857?
quiz.why: The revolt began at Meerut on 10 May 1857.

quiz.q: Who was proclaimed emperor at Delhi during the revolt?
quiz.why: The rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar emperor at Delhi.

quiz.q: Which act of 1858 ended East India Company rule and placed India under the British Crown?
quiz.why: The Government of India Act of 1858 transferred power to the Crown.

centre.show: Enfield Pattern 1853 rifle-musket

sections.title: Social and Religious Reform Movements
sections.intro: Reformers questioned caste, ritual and the treatment of women, and founded schools, societies and new ways of living their faiths.

exhibits.title: Brahmo Samaj
exhibits.text: Founded by Raja Rammohan Roy in 1828, the Brahmo Samaj worshipped one formless God and opposed idol worship, sati and caste. Roy's campaign helped bring about the ban on sati in 1829. Debendranath Tagore and Keshab Chandra Sen carried the movement forward.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Raja Rammohan Roy by Henry Perronet Briggs (1831–32)

exhibits.title: Arya Samaj
exhibits.text: Swami Dayananda Saraswati founded the Arya Samaj in 1875, calling for a return to the Vedas. It opposed idol worship and caste by birth, promoted education through DAV schools and gurukuls, and began the shuddhi movement.
exhibits.show: Photograph/portrait of Swami Dayananda Saraswati; title page of Satyarth Prakash (1875)

exhibits.title: Ramakrishna Mission
exhibits.text: Swami Vivekananda founded the Ramakrishna Mission in 1897 in the name of his teacher, Ramakrishna Paramahamsa. It joins spirituality with social service. Vivekananda's address to the Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893 is famous.
exhibits.show: Photograph of Swami Vivekananda, Chicago 1893 (Parliament of Religions)

exhibits.title: Prarthana Samaj
exhibits.text: The Prarthana Samaj was founded in Bombay in 1867 by Atmaram Pandurang, inspired by the Brahmo Samaj. M. G. Ranade and R. G. Bhandarkar promoted inter-caste dining, widow remarriage and education for women.
exhibits.show: Photograph of Mahadev Govind Ranade

exhibits.title: Aligarh Movement
exhibits.text: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan promoted modern, scientific education among Muslims, founding the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh in 1875. It became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920.
exhibits.show: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan photograph; Strachey Hall, Aligarh Muslim University

exhibits.title: Theosophical Society
exhibits.text: Founded in New York in 1875 by Helena Blavatsky and Henry Olcott, the Theosophical Society moved its headquarters to Adyar in Madras. Annie Besant led it, praised Indian culture, founded the Central Hindu College and later the Home Rule League.
exhibits.show: Photograph of Annie Besant; Theosophical Society headquarters at Adyar, Chennai

exhibits.title: Young Bengal
exhibits.text: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio, a teacher at Hindu College in Calcutta, inspired students in the late 1820s to question tradition and think freely. His followers were known as Young Bengal.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Henry Louis Vivian Derozio (19th-c. lithograph)

exhibits.title: Women reformers
exhibits.text: Savitribai Phule opened schools for girls with Jyotirao Phule from 1848. Pandita Ramabai founded Sharada Sadan for widows, Tarabai Shinde wrote against gender inequality, and Begum Rokeya promoted education for Muslim girls.
exhibits.show: Photograph of Savitribai Phule; Pandita Ramabai photograph

exhibits.title: Education reforms
exhibits.text: Reformers founded schools and colleges for all. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar championed girls' schooling and widow remarriage, legalised in 1856; the Phules opened schools for girls and lower castes; and D. K. Karve founded a university for women in 1916.
exhibits.show: Photograph of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar

quiz.q: Who founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828?
quiz.why: Raja Rammohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828.

quiz.q: Which movement called for a return to the Vedas and began the shuddhi movement?
quiz.why: Dayananda Saraswati's Arya Samaj called for a return to the Vedas.

quiz.q: Where did Sir Syed Ahmad Khan found the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College in 1875?
quiz.why: The college at Aligarh became Aligarh Muslim University in 1920.

centre.show: 19th-century South Indian brass standing oil lamp (kuthuvilakku / deepa)

sections.title: Economic History under British Rule
sections.intro: Colonial rule reshaped India's economy: old industries declined, railways and plantations spread, and famines exposed the costs of empire.

exhibits.title: Early modern industry
exhibits.text: Modern industry began in the 1850s: cotton mills in Bombay from 1854, jute mills in Bengal, coal mining, and later the Tata Iron and Steel Company at Jamshedpur in 1907. Growth was limited and largely in British or a few Indian hands.
exhibits.show: Tata Iron and Steel Works, Jamshedpur – early photograph (c.1910s)

exhibits.title: Deindustrialisation
exhibits.text: Cheap machine-made British cloth and one-sided tariffs ruined many Indian handicraft industries in the 19th century. Weavers of Dhaka and other centres lost their livelihoods, pushing more people into agriculture.
exhibits.show: Dhaka muslin (jamdani) textile, 19th century

exhibits.title: Railways
exhibits.text: The first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853. Railways served British trade and military needs, but also linked markets and people. By 1947 India had one of the largest rail networks in the world.
exhibits.show: Opening of the Great Indian Peninsula Railway, Bombay–Thane, 16 April 1853 (Illustrated London News engraving)

exhibits.title: Famines under British rule
exhibits.text: Repeated famines killed millions, including the Great Famine of 1876 to 1878 and the Bengal Famine of 1943, in which about three million people died. Export policies, high revenue and slow relief made them worse.
exhibits.show: Photograph from the Madras famine of 1876–78 (e.g. relief camp, W. W. Hooper) or the Bengal Famine 1943 (The Statesman)

exhibits.title: Colonial agriculture
exhibits.text: Agriculture stagnated under heavy revenue demands, debt to moneylenders, fragmentation of land and little investment, although canals in Punjab expanded cultivation.
exhibits.show: Persian wheel (rahat) irrigation or Punjab canal headworks, historic photograph

exhibits.title: Commercialisation of agriculture
exhibits.text: Farmers increasingly grew cash crops such as cotton, jute, indigo, opium and groundnut for export, often under pressure. The Indigo Revolt in Bengal, in 1859 and 1860, exposed the coercion used by planters.
exhibits.show: Indigo factory in Bengal, 19th-century lithograph (e.g. Colesworthey Grant, Rural Life in Bengal, 1860)

exhibits.title: Plantation economy
exhibits.text: British planters set up tea plantations in Assam and Bengal, coffee in South India and rubber in Kerala. Indentured workers faced harsh conditions, and Indian labourers were also sent to plantations in Mauritius, Fiji, the Caribbean and Africa.
exhibits.show: Women plucking tea on an Assam tea estate, historic photograph (c.1880–1900)

exhibits.title: Workers and labour
exhibits.text: Mill and plantation workers faced long hours and low pay. Factory Acts from 1881 brought limited protection, trade unions grew, and the All India Trade Union Congress was founded in 1920.
exhibits.show: Bombay cotton mill workers, historic photograph (early 20th century)

exhibits.title: Colonial trade
exhibits.text: India exported raw materials and imported manufactured goods, while its export surpluses helped Britain balance its own trade. The opium trade to China was a major source of Company revenue.
exhibits.show: Stacking room in the opium factory at Patna, lithograph after W. S. Sherwill (c.1850)

quiz.q: Between which two places did India's first passenger train run in 1853?
quiz.why: The first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane on 16 April 1853.

quiz.q: Where was the Tata Iron and Steel Company set up in 1907?
quiz.why: TISCO was established at Jamshedpur in 1907.

quiz.q: The Indigo Revolt of 1859–60 took place in which region?
quiz.why: The Indigo Revolt in Bengal exposed planters' coercion.

centre.show: Fairy Queen, East Indian Railway steam locomotive of 1855 (National Rail Museum, New Delhi)

wings.title: Freedom and the Republic
wings.subtitle: The national movement to modern India
wings.intro: Welcome to Freedom and the Republic: the rise of nationalism, Gandhi and the revolutionaries, partition and independence, the Constitution, and India since 1947.

sections.title: Rise of Nationalism
sections.intro: Shared grievances, new ideas and new organisations turned scattered protest into a national movement for self-government.

exhibits.title: Early nationalism
exhibits.text: Western education, newspapers, railways and shared grievances fostered a national consciousness. Associations such as the British Indian Association, the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha and the Indian Association of 1876 prepared the ground.
exhibits.show: Front page of an early nationalist newspaper such as Tilak's Kesari (1881) or Amrita Bazar Patrika

exhibits.title: Indian National Congress
exhibits.text: The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885 in Bombay, with the help of A. O. Hume, and W. C. Bonnerjee as its first president. It became the main platform of the national movement.
exhibits.show: Group photograph of delegates at the first Indian National Congress session, Bombay, December 1885

exhibits.title: Moderates
exhibits.text: Leaders such as Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta and Gopal Krishna Gokhale used petitions and constitutional methods, demanding reforms, more Indians in the services, and economic justice.
exhibits.show: Portraits of Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale (period photographs)

exhibits.title: Extremists
exhibits.text: Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal, known as Lal, Bal and Pal, demanded swaraj through mass action. Tilak declared that swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it. The Congress split at Surat in 1907.
exhibits.show: Lal-Bal-Pal composite portrait: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal

exhibits.title: Partition of Bengal
exhibits.text: Lord Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905, officially for administrative reasons, but it was widely seen as a move to divide Hindus and Muslims and weaken nationalism. Mass protests forced its reversal in 1911.
exhibits.show: Map of the 1905 Partition of Bengal showing Bengal and the new province of Eastern Bengal and Assam

exhibits.title: Swadeshi Movement
exhibits.text: The Swadeshi movement, from 1905 to 1908, called for the boycott of British goods and the promotion of Indian products, national education and self-help. Rabindranath Tagore's songs and the cry of Bande Mataram rallied the people.
exhibits.show: Abanindranath Tagore's painting 'Bharat Mata' (1905), icon of the Swadeshi movement

exhibits.title: Early revolutionaries
exhibits.text: Some nationalists turned to armed resistance: the Chapekar brothers in 1897, Khudiram Bose and Prafulla Chaki in 1908, the Anushilan Samiti and Jugantar in Bengal, and Abhinav Bharat in Maharashtra.
exhibits.show: Period photograph of Khudiram Bose (1908)

quiz.q: Where was the Indian National Congress founded in December 1885?
quiz.why: The first Congress session met in Bombay in December 1885.

quiz.q: Which three leaders were known together as Lal, Bal and Pal?
options: Tilak, Lajpat Rai and Bipin Chandra Pal
quiz.why: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal led the Extremists.

quiz.q: Which Viceroy partitioned Bengal in 1905?
quiz.why: Lord Curzon carried out the partition, which was reversed in 1911.

centre.show: Madam Bhikaji Cama's 'Flag of Indian Independence' unfurled at Stuttgart, 1907 (green-saffron-red with Vande Mataram)

sections.title: Gandhian Era
sections.intro: Mahatma Gandhi's satyagraha, non-violent resistance, turned the freedom struggle into a mass movement of peasants, workers, women and students.

exhibits.title: Champaran Satyagraha, 1917
exhibits.text: In 1917 Gandhi took up the cause of indigo farmers in Champaran, Bihar, who were forced to grow indigo under the tinkathia system. His first satyagraha in India led to an inquiry and relief for the peasants.
exhibits.show: Photograph of Gandhi at Champaran, Bihar, 1917 (first satyagraha in India)

exhibits.title: Kheda Satyagraha, 1918
exhibits.text: In 1918, after crops failed in Kheda, Gujarat, Gandhi and Vallabhbhai Patel led a satyagraha refusing to pay land tax. The government eased collection for the poorest farmers.
exhibits.show: Period photograph of Gandhi with Vallabhbhai Patel, Gujarat, c.1918 (Kheda Satyagraha)

exhibits.title: Ahmedabad mill strike, 1918
exhibits.text: In 1918 Gandhi supported Ahmedabad mill workers' demand for higher wages and undertook his first fast in India. The dispute ended with a thirty-five per cent wage increase.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Anasuya Sarabhai, who led the 1918 Ahmedabad mill workers, with an early Ahmedabad textile mill

exhibits.title: Non-Cooperation Movement
exhibits.text: Launched in 1920 after the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and alongside the Khilafat movement, it urged Indians to boycott foreign goods, courts, schools and titles. Gandhi called it off in 1922 after the violence at Chauri Chaura.
exhibits.show: Bonfire of foreign cloth during the Non-Cooperation Movement, c.1921 (photograph)

exhibits.title: Civil Disobedience Movement
exhibits.text: After the Lahore Congress demanded Purna Swaraj, complete independence, in 1929, Gandhi began the Civil Disobedience Movement in 1930, urging people to break unjust laws. It paused with the Gandhi–Irwin Pact of 1931 and resumed in 1932.
exhibits.show: Women volunteers picketing foreign-cloth or liquor shops, Bombay, 1930

exhibits.title: The Salt March
exhibits.text: From 12 March to 6 April 1930, Gandhi walked 385 kilometres from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi and made salt from the sea, defying the salt tax. Thousands followed, and the march drew worldwide attention.
exhibits.show: Gandhi picking up salt at Dandi, 6 April 1930 photograph (alt: Gandhi walking with staff on the march)

exhibits.title: Round Table Conferences
exhibits.text: Three Round Table Conferences in London, from 1930 to 1932, discussed constitutional reform. The Congress attended only the second, represented by Gandhi. Disagreement over minority representation led to the Communal Award and the Poona Pact of 1932.
exhibits.show: Gandhi at the Second Round Table Conference, St James's Palace, London, 1931

exhibits.title: Quit India Movement
exhibits.text: On 8 August 1942 the Congress launched the Quit India Movement, with Gandhi's call to do or die. Leaders were arrested at once, but people struck, protested and set up parallel governments in places such as Satara and Ballia.
exhibits.show: Crowds at Gowalia Tank Maidan (August Kranti Maidan), Bombay, at the Quit India session, 8 August 1942

quiz.q: Where did Gandhi lead his first satyagraha in India in 1917?
quiz.why: He took up the cause of indigo farmers in Champaran, Bihar.

quiz.q: Why did Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in 1922?
quiz.why: He suspended it after the violence at Chauri Chaura.

quiz.q: Where did the Salt March of 1930 end?
quiz.why: Gandhi walked from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi and made salt from the sea.

centre.show: Gandhi's portable box charkha (Yerawada-type folding spinning wheel), as preserved at Sabarmati Ashram

sections.title: Revolutionary Nationalism
sections.intro: Alongside non-violent mass movements, revolutionaries in India and abroad took up arms against British rule.

exhibits.title: Anushilan Samiti
exhibits.text: The Anushilan Samiti began in Bengal in 1902 as a physical-training society and became a revolutionary organisation. With Jugantar, it carried out attacks on officials; the Alipore Bomb Case of 1908 involved Aurobindo Ghosh.
exhibits.show: Group photograph of the Alipore Bomb Case accused (1908), linked to Anushilan/Jugantar

exhibits.title: Hindustan Socialist Republican Association
exhibits.text: Founded in 1924 as the Hindustan Republican Association, it carried out the Kakori train action in 1925. Renamed the Hindustan Socialist Republican Association in 1928, under Chandrashekhar Azad and Bhagat Singh, it adopted socialist aims.
exhibits.show: Portraits of Ram Prasad Bismil and Ashfaqulla Khan, leaders of the 1925 Kakori train action

exhibits.title: Bhagat Singh
exhibits.text: Bhagat Singh, who lived from 1907 to 1931, took part in the killing of police officer Saunders in 1928 to avenge Lala Lajpat Rai, and threw harmless bombs in the Central Legislative Assembly in 1929 to make the deaf hear. He was hanged with Rajguru and Sukhdev on 23 March 1931.
exhibits.show: Bhagat Singh's 1929 photograph in a felt hat (taken in Delhi)

exhibits.title: Chandrashekhar Azad
exhibits.text: Chandrashekhar Azad led the HSRA and took part in the Kakori action. Vowing never to be captured alive, he died fighting police in Alfred Park, Allahabad, in 1931; the park now bears his name.
exhibits.show: Chandrashekhar Azad's well-known photograph twirling his moustache

exhibits.title: Surya Sen
exhibits.text: Surya Sen, known as Masterda, led the Chittagong Armoury Raid in April 1930 with the Indian Republican Army, which included young women such as Pritilata Waddedar and Kalpana Dutt. He was hanged in 1934.
exhibits.show: Portrait photograph of Surya Sen (Masterda)

exhibits.title: Ghadar Movement
exhibits.text: The Ghadar Party was founded in 1913 in San Francisco by Indian migrants, including Lala Har Dayal and Sohan Singh Bhakna. During the First World War it attempted an uprising in India in 1915, which was crushed.
exhibits.show: Front page of the Ghadar Party newspaper 'Hindustan Ghadar' (San Francisco, 1913–14)

exhibits.title: Indian National Army
exhibits.text: The Indian National Army was formed in South-East Asia in 1942 with Japanese support and revived by Subhas Chandra Bose in 1943, with the slogan Delhi Chalo. The INA trials at the Red Fort in 1945 and 1946 stirred nationwide support.
exhibits.show: Subhas Chandra Bose inspecting INA troops / Rani of Jhansi Regiment, c.1943

exhibits.title: Subhas Chandra Bose
exhibits.text: Subhas Chandra Bose, twice president of the Congress, formed the Forward Bloc, escaped from house arrest in 1941, and led the Indian National Army and the Provisional Government of Free India. He is reported to have died after a plane crash in Taiwan in August 1945.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose in INA uniform

quiz.q: Which revolutionary led the Chittagong Armoury Raid of April 1930?
quiz.why: Surya Sen, known as Masterda, led the raid.

quiz.q: In which city was the Ghadar Party founded in 1913?
quiz.why: Indian migrants founded it in San Francisco.

quiz.q: What was the slogan of the Indian National Army under Subhas Chandra Bose?
quiz.why: Bose rallied the INA with the call Delhi Chalo.

centre.show: Cellular Jail, Port Blair (Kala Pani), central tower with radiating wings, where revolutionaries were imprisoned

sections.title: Constitutional Development
sections.intro: Acts of the British Parliament slowly added Indian voices to government, and finally an Indian Constituent Assembly wrote the country's own constitution.

exhibits.title: Regulating Act, 1773
exhibits.text: The Regulating Act of 1773 was Parliament's first step to control the Company. It made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General, the first being Warren Hastings, with a council, and set up a Supreme Court at Calcutta.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Warren Hastings, first Governor-General (e.g. by Tilly Kettle, c.1772)

exhibits.title: Pitt's India Act, 1784
exhibits.text: Pitt's India Act of 1784 created a Board of Control in London to supervise the Company's political affairs, establishing dual control by the Company and the British government.
exhibits.show: Portrait of William Pitt the Younger, whose government passed the 1784 India Act

exhibits.title: Charter Acts
exhibits.text: Charter Acts renewed the Company's charter. The Act of 1813 ended its trade monopoly except in tea and with China and set aside money for education; 1833 created the Governor-General of India and ended its trade; 1853 opened the civil services to competition.
exhibits.show: East India House, Leadenhall Street, London (period engraving/painting)

exhibits.title: Indian Councils Acts, 1861 and 1892
exhibits.text: The Indian Councils Acts of 1861 and 1892 added nominated, and later indirectly elected, Indian members to legislative councils, giving a limited voice but no real power.
exhibits.show: Photograph of the Imperial Legislative Council in session, Calcutta (late 19th / early 20th c.)

exhibits.title: Morley–Minto Reforms, 1909
exhibits.text: The Indian Councils Act of 1909 enlarged the councils and introduced separate electorates for Muslims, a step criticised for deepening communal divisions.
exhibits.show: Portraits of John Morley (Secretary of State) and Lord Minto (Viceroy)

exhibits.title: Montagu–Chelmsford Reforms, 1919
exhibits.text: The Government of India Act of 1919 introduced dyarchy in the provinces, with some subjects handed to elected ministers, a two-house central legislature and a limited franchise.
exhibits.show: Title page of the 'Report on Indian Constitutional Reforms' (Montagu–Chelmsford Report, 1918)

exhibits.title: Government of India Act 1935
exhibits.text: The Government of India Act of 1935 gave the provinces autonomy, proposed an all-India federation, set up a Federal Court and widened the franchise. Many of its features passed into the Constitution of India.
exhibits.show: Title page of the Government of India Act, 1935 (printed statute)

exhibits.title: Cabinet Mission, 1946
exhibits.text: In 1946 a British Cabinet Mission proposed a united India with a limited centre, groupings of provinces and a Constituent Assembly. Disputes over its meaning led to the Muslim League's Direct Action Day.
exhibits.show: Photograph of the Cabinet Mission (Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, A. V. Alexander) in Delhi, 1946

exhibits.title: Constituent Assembly
exhibits.text: Elected indirectly by the provincial assemblies in 1946, the Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946, with Dr Rajendra Prasad as its president. Over nearly three years it debated and adopted the Constitution.
exhibits.show: Photograph of the first session of the Constituent Assembly, 9 December 1946, Constitution Hall, New Delhi

quiz.q: Who became the first Governor-General under the Regulating Act of 1773?
quiz.why: The Act made the Governor of Bengal, Warren Hastings, Governor-General.

quiz.q: Which reform introduced separate electorates for Muslims?
quiz.why: The Indian Councils Act of 1909 introduced separate electorates.

quiz.q: Who was president of the Constituent Assembly when it first met on 9 December 1946?
quiz.why: Dr Rajendra Prasad was the Constituent Assembly's president.

centre.show: Old Parliament House (Council House), New Delhi, built 1921–27 by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker for the legislature

sections.title: Partition and Independence
sections.intro: Independence came in August 1947 together with the partition of the subcontinent, one of the largest and most painful migrations in history.

exhibits.title: Two-Nation Theory
exhibits.text: The two-nation theory held that Hindus and Muslims formed separate nations. It was advanced by Muhammad Ali Jinnah and the Muslim League in the 1940s. The Congress and many Indians rejected it.
exhibits.show: Gandhi and Jinnah during their talks in Bombay, September 1944

exhibits.title: Muslim League
exhibits.text: The All-India Muslim League was founded in Dhaka in 1906. At first seeking safeguards for Muslims, under Jinnah it demanded a separate state, Pakistan, and won most Muslim seats in the 1946 elections.
exhibits.show: Ahsan Manzil, Dhaka, associated with the founding of the All-India Muslim League in 1906

exhibits.title: Lahore Resolution
exhibits.text: On 23 March 1940, at Lahore, the Muslim League demanded independent states for Muslim-majority areas in the north-west and east of India. It is often called the Pakistan Resolution.
exhibits.show: Minar-e-Pakistan, Lahore, built at the site (Minto Park, now Iqbal Park) where the 1940 resolution was passed

exhibits.title: Mountbatten Plan
exhibits.text: The plan of 3 June 1947 by the Viceroy, Lord Mountbatten, provided for partition, with Punjab and Bengal divided, and an early transfer of power. The Indian Independence Act of July 1947 put it into effect.
exhibits.show: Mountbatten meeting Indian leaders (Nehru, Jinnah, Patel and others) to discuss the plan, Delhi, 2 June 1947

exhibits.title: Partition
exhibits.text: Sir Cyril Radcliffe drew the new boundaries in about five weeks, and the Radcliffe Line was announced on 17 August 1947. Punjab and Bengal were divided, creating West and East Pakistan.
exhibits.show: Map of the Radcliffe Award boundaries in Punjab, 1947 (with Bengal inset)

exhibits.title: Refugee crisis
exhibits.text: Partition caused one of history's largest migrations: about fifteen million people crossed the new borders, and communal violence killed hundreds of thousands, perhaps up to a million or more. Refugee relief and resettlement became urgent tasks.
exhibits.show: Photograph of refugee trains/convoys crossing Punjab, 1947

exhibits.title: Independence
exhibits.text: At midnight on 14 to 15 August 1947 India became independent. Jawaharlal Nehru, the first Prime Minister, spoke of India's tryst with destiny. Lord Mountbatten stayed on as Governor-General, followed by C. Rajagopalachari.
exhibits.show: Nehru delivering the 'Tryst with Destiny' speech, Constituent Assembly, midnight 14–15 August 1947

quiz.q: Where was the All-India Muslim League founded in 1906?
quiz.why: The League was founded in Dhaka in 1906.

quiz.q: Who drew the boundary lines that partitioned Punjab and Bengal?
quiz.why: Sir Cyril Radcliffe drew the Radcliffe Line in about five weeks.

quiz.q: About how many people crossed the new borders during Partition?
quiz.why: About fifteen million people migrated across the new borders.

centre.show: Map of the Radcliffe Line, August 1947, showing the partition of Punjab and Bengal

sections.title: Integration of Princely States
sections.intro: More than five hundred princely states had to be brought into the new nation. Most joined peacefully; a few did not.

exhibits.title: Sardar Patel
exhibits.text: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, led the integration of over five hundred princely states into India through persuasion and, where needed, firmness. He is called the Iron Man of India.
exhibits.show: Portrait photograph of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, c.1947–49

exhibits.title: V. P. Menon
exhibits.text: V. P. Menon, secretary of the States Ministry, drafted the Instrument of Accession and negotiated with rulers alongside Patel. He wrote The Story of the Integration of the Indian States.
exhibits.show: Portrait of V. P. Menon; cover of his book 'The Story of the Integration of the Indian States' (1956)

exhibits.title: Hyderabad, 1948
exhibits.text: The Nizam of Hyderabad sought to stay independent. Amid violence by the Razakars, India launched Operation Polo in September 1948, and Hyderabad was integrated within days.
exhibits.show: Nizam Mir Osman Ali Khan meeting Sardar Patel at Begumpet airport, Hyderabad, after integration (1948–49)

exhibits.title: Junagadh
exhibits.text: The Nawab of Junagadh acceded to Pakistan, though most of his people were Hindu and the state was surrounded by India. After popular protest and Indian action, a plebiscite in February 1948 favoured India.
exhibits.show: Mahabat Maqbara mausoleum, Junagadh (19th c.), emblem of the princely state

exhibits.title: Kashmir
exhibits.text: Maharaja Hari Singh signed the Instrument of Accession to India in October 1947, after tribal raiders from Pakistan invaded. War followed, and a UN-brokered ceasefire in January 1949 left the region divided.
exhibits.show: Instrument of Accession signed by Maharaja Hari Singh, 26 October 1947

quiz.q: Who is known as the Iron Man of India for integrating the princely states?
quiz.why: Sardar Patel led the integration of over five hundred princely states.

quiz.q: What was the 1948 military action that integrated Hyderabad called?
quiz.why: India launched Operation Polo in September 1948.

quiz.q: Who signed the Instrument of Accession for Kashmir in October 1947?
quiz.why: Maharaja Hari Singh acceded to India after raiders invaded.

centre.show: Statue of Unity, Kevadia, Gujarat (Sardar Patel, 182 m, inaugurated 2018)

sections.title: Constitution of India
sections.intro: The Constitution of India, adopted in 1949, created a sovereign democratic republic and set out the rights of citizens and the duties of the state.

exhibits.title: Drafting Committee
exhibits.text: Chaired by Dr B. R. Ambedkar, the Drafting Committee prepared the draft Constitution. Adopted on 26 November 1949, it came into force on 26 January 1950, now celebrated as Republic Day.
exhibits.show: Dr B. R. Ambedkar with members of the Drafting Committee (group photograph, c.1947–49)

exhibits.title: Fundamental Rights
exhibits.text: Part Three guarantees fundamental rights: equality, freedoms such as speech and expression, protection of life and liberty, rights against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and constitutional remedies under Article 32, which Ambedkar called the heart and soul of the Constitution.
exhibits.show: Illustrated opening of Part III (Fundamental Rights) in the original Constitution – Ram, Sita and Lakshmana scene

exhibits.title: Directive Principles of State Policy
exhibits.text: Part Four sets out Directive Principles of State Policy: goals of social and economic justice, such as adequate livelihood, equal pay for equal work, education and village panchayats. They cannot be enforced in court but are fundamental to governance.
exhibits.show: Illustrated opening of Part IV (Directive Principles) in the original Constitution – Krishna counselling Arjuna

exhibits.title: Fundamental Duties
exhibits.text: Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976, on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee. Article 51A now lists eleven duties, such as respecting the Constitution and protecting the environment.
exhibits.show: Text of Article 51A (Fundamental Duties) from the Constitution as amended by the 42nd Amendment, 1976

exhibits.title: Indian federalism
exhibits.text: India is a Union of States with a strong centre. Powers are divided into Union, State and Concurrent lists, with an independent judiciary. Scholars describe it as quasi-federal or as cooperative federalism.
exhibits.show: Political map of India's states and union territories (official Survey of India map)

exhibits.title: Amendment process
exhibits.text: Article 368 allows Parliament to amend the Constitution, some changes also needing ratification by the states. In the Kesavananda Bharati case of 1973, the Supreme Court held that the basic structure of the Constitution cannot be destroyed.
exhibits.show: Supreme Court of India building, New Delhi (scales-of-justice plan, opened 1958)

quiz.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution?
quiz.why: Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.

quiz.q: Which amendment added Fundamental Duties to the Constitution in 1976?
quiz.why: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 added Article 51A.

quiz.q: Which 1973 case established that the basic structure of the Constitution cannot be destroyed?
quiz.why: The Supreme Court laid down the basic structure doctrine in Kesavananda Bharati.

centre.show: Original handwritten Constitution of India (calligraphy by Prem Behari Narain Raizada, illustrations by Nandalal Bose and Santiniketan artists)

sections.title: Independent India
sections.intro: Since 1947 India has built a democracy, planned its development, fed itself, opened its economy and changed in countless ways.

exhibits.title: Nehru Era
exhibits.text: Jawaharlal Nehru, Prime Minister from 1947 to 1964, built democratic institutions, a mixed economy, scientific and technical institutions such as the IITs, and a foreign policy of non-alignment. The first general elections were held in 1951 and 1952.
exhibits.show: Nehru at the Bhakra Nangal Dam, which he called a 'temple of modern India'

exhibits.title: Five-Year Plans
exhibits.text: Planning began with the First Five-Year Plan in 1951, focused on agriculture; the Second, from 1956, based on the Mahalanobis model, stressed heavy industry. The Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog in 2015.
exhibits.show: Bhilai Steel Plant (Second Five-Year Plan, built with Soviet aid) – period photograph

exhibits.title: Green Revolution
exhibits.text: From the mid-1960s, high-yielding wheat and rice, irrigation and fertilisers raised harvests, especially in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh. The scientist M. S. Swaminathan is closely associated with it, and India became self-sufficient in food grains.
exhibits.show: Indian 1968 'Wheat Revolution' commemorative postage stamp (alt: M. S. Swaminathan with Norman Borlaug in wheat fields)

exhibits.title: White Revolution
exhibits.text: Operation Flood, launched in 1970 under Verghese Kurien, built a national network of milk cooperatives on the model of Amul at Anand. India became the world's largest producer of milk.
exhibits.show: Amul dairy at Anand / portrait of Verghese Kurien, with traditional aluminium milk cans

exhibits.title: Bank nationalisation
exhibits.text: In July 1969 Indira Gandhi's government nationalised fourteen major banks to extend credit to agriculture and small businesses; six more followed in 1980.
exhibits.show: Newspaper front page announcing nationalisation of 14 banks, 19–20 July 1969

exhibits.title: The Emergency, 1975–77
exhibits.text: On 25 June 1975 a national Emergency was declared, citing internal disturbance. Civil liberties were suspended, opposition leaders jailed and the press censored. It ended in 1977, and the Janata Party won the elections that followed.
exhibits.show: Indian Express front page with a blank editorial protesting censorship, June 1975

exhibits.title: Liberalisation, 1991
exhibits.text: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis in 1991, the government of P. V. Narasimha Rao, with Finance Minister Manmohan Singh, devalued the rupee, dismantled industrial licensing, opened the economy to foreign investment and cut tariffs.
exhibits.show: Finance Minister Manmohan Singh presenting the Union Budget, 24 July 1991

exhibits.title: Coalition politics
exhibits.text: From 1989, no single party won a Lok Sabha majority for twenty-five years. Coalitions such as the National Front, United Front, NDA and UPA governed, giving regional parties greater influence. A single-party majority returned in 2014.
exhibits.show: Electronic Voting Machine (EVM) – ballot and control units used in Indian elections

exhibits.title: Continuing economic reform
exhibits.text: Reforms continued with privatisation, growth in telecom and information technology, the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code of 2016, the Goods and Services Tax of 2017 and the spread of digital payments, making India one of the fastest-growing large economies.
exhibits.show: GST launch at midnight in Parliament's Central Hall, 30 June–1 July 2017

quiz.q: Which scientist is most closely associated with India's Green Revolution?
quiz.why: M. S. Swaminathan is closely associated with the Green Revolution.

quiz.q: In which year did Indira Gandhi's government nationalise fourteen major banks?
quiz.why: Fourteen banks were nationalised in July 1969.

quiz.q: Who was Finance Minister during the 1991 liberalisation?
quiz.why: Manmohan Singh was Finance Minister under P. V. Narasimha Rao.

centre.show: A 1960s–70s farm tractor of the Green Revolution era in Punjab

wings.title: Themes of Indian History
wings.subtitle: Ideas that run through the ages
wings.intro: Welcome to the Themes gallery: foreign policy, science, art and culture, religion, economy, society, and how historians have written India's story.

sections.title: Foreign Policy
sections.intro: Independent India sought its own path in world affairs, from non-alignment and the wars on its borders to its growing global role today.

exhibits.title: Non-Aligned Movement
exhibits.text: India helped found the Non-Aligned Movement with Yugoslavia, Egypt, Indonesia and Ghana; its first summit was held in Belgrade in 1961. It sought independence from both Cold War blocs.
exhibits.show: Leaders at the first Non-Aligned summit, Belgrade, September 1961 (Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno, Nkrumah)

exhibits.title: Panchsheel
exhibits.text: The five principles of peaceful coexistence were set out in the 1954 agreement between India and China: mutual respect for territory and sovereignty, non-aggression, non-interference, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence.
exhibits.show: Nehru with Zhou Enlai during Zhou's visit to India, June 1954 (Panchsheel era)

exhibits.title: Indo-China War, 1962
exhibits.text: Border disputes over Aksai Chin and the McMahon Line led to war in October and November 1962. China advanced and then declared a ceasefire. The defeat led India to strengthen its defences.
exhibits.show: Map of the Sino-Indian border: Aksai Chin (western sector) and McMahon Line (eastern sector), 1962

exhibits.title: India–Pakistan wars
exhibits.text: India and Pakistan fought wars in 1947 to 1948 and in 1965 over Kashmir, in 1971 over Bangladesh, and at Kargil in 1999. The Tashkent Agreement of 1966 and the Shimla Agreement of 1972 followed the earlier wars.
exhibits.show: Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto at the Shimla Agreement, July 1972

exhibits.title: Bangladesh Liberation War
exhibits.text: In 1971, after Pakistan's crackdown in East Pakistan and the flight of about ten million refugees to India, India supported the Mukti Bahini and went to war. Pakistan's forces surrendered at Dhaka on 16 December 1971, and Bangladesh was born.
exhibits.show: Lt Gen A. A. K. Niazi signing the Instrument of Surrender beside Lt Gen J. S. Aurora, Dhaka, 16 Dec 1971

exhibits.title: India's nuclear programme
exhibits.text: Homi Bhabha founded India's atomic energy programme. India conducted a nuclear test at Pokhran in 1974 and further tests in 1998, declaring itself a nuclear weapons state with a policy of no first use.
exhibits.show: PM Vajpayee with A. P. J. Abdul Kalam at the Pokhran test site after Pokhran-II, May 1998

exhibits.title: Look East and Act East
exhibits.text: The Look East Policy of 1991 built economic links with South-East Asia. In 2014 it became Act East, adding strategic and connectivity goals with ASEAN and the wider Indo-Pacific.
exhibits.show: Map of India and the ten ASEAN states, with the India–Myanmar–Thailand Trilateral Highway

exhibits.title: Contemporary diplomacy
exhibits.text: Today India engages through groups such as the G20, which it hosted in 2023, BRICS, the Quad and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, contributes to UN peacekeeping, and seeks a permanent seat on the UN Security Council.
exhibits.show: G20 leaders at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi summit, September 2023

quiz.q: Where was the first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement held in 1961?
quiz.why: The first Non-Aligned summit took place in Belgrade in 1961.

quiz.q: The Panchsheel principles of 1954 were set out in an agreement between India and which country?
quiz.why: Panchsheel was set out in the 1954 India–China agreement.

quiz.q: Which agreement followed the 1971 war between India and Pakistan?
quiz.why: The Shimla Agreement of 1972 followed the 1971 war; Tashkent followed 1965.

centre.show: Nehru with Nasser and Tito at Brioni, July 1956 (wall image); pedestal: mid-20th-century desk globe

sections.title: Science and Technology
sections.intro: From atomic energy to Moon landings and digital payments, India has built world-class science and technology institutions.

exhibits.title: Indian Space Research Organisation
exhibits.text: The Indian Space Research Organisation, founded in 1969 from Vikram Sarabhai's vision, builds launch vehicles such as the PSLV and GSLV and satellites for communication, weather, earth observation and navigation.
exhibits.show: Vikram Sarabhai portrait with early sounding rocket at Thumba (TERLS), 1960s

exhibits.title: Defence Research and Development Organisation
exhibits.text: The Defence Research and Development Organisation, formed in 1958, develops defence technology, including the Agni and Prithvi missiles of the programme led by A. P. J. Abdul Kalam, and the Tejas light combat aircraft.
exhibits.show: HAL Tejas light combat aircraft in flight (or Agni missile at Republic Day parade)

exhibits.title: Nuclear energy
exhibits.text: India follows a three-stage nuclear power programme planned by Homi Bhabha to make use of its large thorium reserves. Its first research reactor, Apsara, started in 1956, and the Tarapur power station in 1969.
exhibits.show: Tarapur Atomic Power Station, Maharashtra (India's first nuclear power station, 1969)

exhibits.title: India's space missions
exhibits.text: Highlights include the satellite Aryabhata in 1975; Chandrayaan-1 in 2008, which found evidence of water on the Moon; Mangalyaan in 2013, the first Asian mission to reach Mars orbit; Chandrayaan-3's landing near the lunar south pole in 2023; and Aditya-L1, studying the Sun.
exhibits.show: Chandrayaan-3 Vikram lander on the Moon, imaged by the Pragyan rover's NavCam, August 2023

exhibits.title: Digital India
exhibits.text: Launched in 2015, Digital India expands internet access and online public services. The Aadhaar digital identity and the Unified Payments Interface, or UPI, have made India a world leader in digital payments.
exhibits.show: UPI QR code payment at a street vendor's stall

quiz.q: In which year was the Indian Space Research Organisation founded?
quiz.why: ISRO was founded in 1969 from Vikram Sarabhai's vision.

quiz.q: Homi Bhabha's three-stage nuclear power programme aims to use India's large reserves of which element?
quiz.why: The programme is planned to make use of India's large thorium reserves.

quiz.q: Which mission landed near the lunar south pole in 2023?
quiz.why: Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023.

centre.show: PSLV on the launch pad at Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, ISRO photo

sections.title: Art and Culture
sections.intro: India's art and culture span thousands of years and hundreds of traditions, from cave paintings and temples to classical dance, music and film.

exhibits.title: Indian architecture
exhibits.text: From Harappan cities and Buddhist stupas to Hindu temples, Indo-Islamic tombs, Mughal gardens, colonial buildings and modern Chandigarh, India's architecture is rich and varied, with more than forty UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
exhibits.show: Taj Mahal, Agra, from the Charbagh garden axis

exhibits.title: Indian sculpture
exhibits.text: Traditions range from the Harappan bronze dancer and polished Mauryan stone to the Buddhas of Gandhara and Mathura, Gupta images, the rock-cut panels of Elephanta and Ellora, and Chola bronzes.
exhibits.show: Bronze 'Dancing Girl' of Mohenjo-daro (National Museum, New Delhi)

exhibits.title: Indian painting
exhibits.text: Indian painting includes the Ajanta murals, Pala manuscripts, Mughal, Rajput and Pahari miniatures, the Tanjore and Kalighat schools, folk forms such as Madhubani, Warli and Pattachitra, and modern artists such as Raja Ravi Varma and Amrita Sher-Gil.
exhibits.show: Bodhisattva Padmapani mural, Ajanta Cave 1

exhibits.title: Indian dance
exhibits.text: Classical dance forms include Bharatanatyam, Kathak, Kathakali, Kuchipudi, Odissi, Manipuri, Mohiniyattam and Sattriya, alongside many folk dances. Bharata's Natyashastra is the ancient treatise on performance.
exhibits.show: Natyashastra karana dance reliefs on the gopuram of the Nataraja Temple, Chidambaram

exhibits.title: Indian music
exhibits.text: Indian classical music has two great traditions: Hindustani in the north and Carnatic in the south, both built on raga, melody, and tala, rhythm. Tansen, Tyagaraja, Ravi Shankar and M. S. Subbulakshmi are among its celebrated musicians.
exhibits.show: Ragamala miniature painting (e.g. Todi Ragini), Rajput or Deccani school

exhibits.title: Indian theatre
exhibits.text: Sanskrit drama flourished with Bhasa, Kalidasa and Bhavabhuti. Folk theatre includes Yakshagana, Jatra, Nautanki and Tamasha, and modern theatre grew with groups such as IPTA and institutions like the National School of Drama.
exhibits.show: Yakshagana performer in full costume and headdress, coastal Karnataka

exhibits.title: Indian literature
exhibits.text: Indian literature spans the Vedas and the epics, Sangam poetry, Sanskrit kavya, bhakti verse, Persian and Urdu poetry, and modern writing in many languages. Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.
exhibits.show: Rabindranath Tagore portrait, c. 1913 (Nobel year)

exhibits.title: Languages of India
exhibits.text: India's languages belong mainly to the Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austroasiatic and Tibeto-Burman families. The Eighth Schedule of the Constitution lists twenty-two languages; Hindi in the Devanagari script is the official language of the Union, with English also used.
exhibits.show: Map of India's language families (Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austroasiatic, Tibeto-Burman)

exhibits.title: Festivals of India
exhibits.text: Festivals such as Diwali, Holi, Eid, Christmas, Durga Puja, Pongal, Onam, Baisakhi, Navratri and Buddha Purnima reflect India's diversity. The Kumbh Mela and Durga Puja in Kolkata are recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage.
exhibits.show: Durga Puja pandal and idol in Kolkata (UNESCO intangible heritage, 2021)

quiz.q: Which ancient treatise on performance is attributed to Bharata?
quiz.why: Bharata's Natyashastra is the ancient treatise on performance.

quiz.q: In which year did Rabindranath Tagore win the Nobel Prize in Literature?
quiz.why: Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.

quiz.q: How many languages are listed in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution?
quiz.why: The Eighth Schedule lists twenty-two languages.

centre.show: Chola bronze Shiva Nataraja (11th c.), e.g. the one in the Rijksmuseum or Cleveland Museum of Art

sections.title: Religion in India
sections.intro: India is the birthplace of four world religions and home to many others that arrived over the centuries, living side by side.

exhibits.title: Hinduism
exhibits.text: Hinduism, followed by about four in five Indians, is a family of traditions rooted in the Vedas, the epics and the Puranas, including Vaishnava, Shaiva and Shakta paths and many schools of philosophy. Central ideas include dharma, karma and moksha.
exhibits.show: Meenakshi Amman Temple gopurams, Madurai

exhibits.title: Buddhism in India today
exhibits.text: Born in India, Buddhism declined here after about the 12th century but flourished across Asia. In 1956 Dr B. R. Ambedkar and hundreds of thousands of his followers embraced Buddhism at Nagpur, reviving it in India.
exhibits.show: Dr B. R. Ambedkar at the Deeksha (conversion) ceremony, Nagpur, 14 October 1956

exhibits.title: Jainism in India today
exhibits.text: Jains are a small but influential community, known for ahimsa, vegetarianism, philanthropy and business. Temples at Palitana, Ranakpur and Dilwara, and the statue of Gommateshwara at Shravanabelagola are famous.
exhibits.show: Gommateshwara (Bahubali) monolith, Shravanabelagola, c. 983 CE

exhibits.title: Sikhism
exhibits.text: Founded by Guru Nanak and shaped by ten Gurus, Sikhism teaches devotion to one God, equality and selfless service. The Guru Granth Sahib is its eternal Guru, and the Harmandir Sahib, the Golden Temple at Amritsar, is its holiest shrine.
exhibits.show: Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple), Amritsar, across the Amrit Sarovar

exhibits.title: Islam in India
exhibits.text: Islam reached India through Arab traders on the Kerala coast in the 7th century, and later through conquest and Sufi saints. India has one of the largest Muslim populations in the world, about one in seven Indians.
exhibits.show: Jama Masjid, Delhi (Shah Jahan, 1650s)

exhibits.title: Christianity in India
exhibits.text: Tradition holds that Saint Thomas the Apostle came to Kerala in 52 CE, and Syrian Christians trace their faith to him. Later missionaries spread Christianity further, and Christian institutions contributed to education and healthcare.
exhibits.show: San Thome Basilica, Chennai, built over the traditional tomb of St Thomas

exhibits.title: Zoroastrianism
exhibits.text: Zoroastrians from Persia settled in Gujarat around the 8th to 10th centuries, becoming the Parsis. Though few in number, Parsis have shaped modern India; they include Dadabhai Naoroji and the Tata family.
exhibits.show: Iranshah Atash Behram, Udvada, Gujarat (exterior)

exhibits.title: Judaism in India
exhibits.text: Jewish communities in India include the Cochin Jews of Kerala, the Bene Israel of Maharashtra and the Baghdadi Jews. The Paradesi Synagogue in Kochi dates from 1568. Indian Jews lived for centuries without persecution.
exhibits.show: Paradesi Synagogue, Kochi: interior with Chinese hand-painted tiles and glass chandeliers

quiz.q: Where did Dr B. R. Ambedkar and his followers embrace Buddhism in 1956?
quiz.why: The 1956 conversion ceremony took place at Nagpur.

quiz.q: In which Indian state did Zoroastrians from Persia settle, becoming the Parsis?
quiz.why: Zoroastrian settlers arrived in Gujarat around the 8th to 10th centuries.

quiz.q: The Paradesi Synagogue, dating from 1568, is in which city?
quiz.why: The Paradesi Synagogue is in Kochi, Kerala.

sections.title: Indian Economy Through History
sections.intro: From Harappan seals to UPI, trade, coins, guilds and banks tell the story of India's economic life over five thousand years.

exhibits.title: Ancient trade
exhibits.text: Harappans traded with Mesopotamia; later India traded with Persia, Greece, Rome, China and South-East Asia, exporting spices, textiles, gems and ivory. The Roman writer Pliny complained of Roman gold flowing to India.
exhibits.show: Roman silver denarii of Augustus/Tiberius found in South Indian hoards

exhibits.title: Medieval trade
exhibits.text: Medieval India exported cotton textiles, indigo, sugar and spices, and imported horses, silver and luxury goods. Cities such as Delhi, Agra, Cambay, Surat and Masulipatnam were busy centres of commerce.
exhibits.show: Painted and dyed cotton chintz from the Coromandel Coast, 17th–18th century

exhibits.title: Maritime trade
exhibits.text: Indian Ocean trade linked India with Arabia, East Africa, South-East Asia and China, with the monsoon winds setting the sailing seasons. Gujarati, Tamil and Arab merchants were especially active on these routes.
exhibits.show: Map of Indian Ocean trade routes with summer and winter monsoon winds

exhibits.title: Guilds
exhibits.text: Guilds of merchants and craftspeople, called shrenis, regulated work, quality and prices, acted as banks and gave donations to temples and monasteries. South Indian merchant guilds such as the Ainnurruvar and Manigramam traded across the seas.
exhibits.show: Inscription by the ivory-carvers of Vidisha on the south gateway of the Great Stupa, Sanchi

exhibits.title: Indian coinage
exhibits.text: India's first coins were punch-marked silver coins, from about the 6th century BCE. Indo-Greek and Kushana coins introduced royal portraits, the Guptas issued gold dinaras, and Sher Shah Suri introduced the rupiya, ancestor of today's rupee.
exhibits.show: Silver rupiya of Sher Shah Suri (1540s)

exhibits.title: Taxation through history
exhibits.text: Ancient texts mention bhaga, a share of the produce, as tax; the Mauryas and later states took around a sixth to a quarter. Akbar's zabt and colonial land revenue followed, and the Goods and Services Tax of 2017 unified indirect taxes.
exhibits.show: Illustrated manuscript page of the Ain-i-Akbari (Abu'l Fazl), Akbar's administration

exhibits.title: Banking through history
exhibits.text: Moneylenders and indigenous bankers used hundis, bills of exchange, for centuries. Modern banks include the Bank of Hindustan of 1770, the Presidency banks and the Reserve Bank of India, founded in 1935 and nationalised in 1949.
exhibits.show: A 19th-century hundi (indigenous bill of exchange)

exhibits.title: Industrialisation since independence
exhibits.text: After independence India built steel plants, dams and public-sector industries. Since 1991 private industry, services and information technology have driven growth, and India is now among the world's largest economies.
exhibits.show: Bhakra Dam, Himachal Pradesh (Nehru's 'temples of modern India')

quiz.q: Who introduced the rupiya, ancestor of today's rupee?
quiz.why: Sher Shah Suri introduced the silver rupiya.

quiz.q: What were guilds of merchants and craftspeople called in ancient India?
quiz.why: Guilds were called shrenis; hundis were bills of exchange.

quiz.q: In which year was the Reserve Bank of India founded?
quiz.why: The RBI was founded in 1935 and nationalised in 1949.

sections.title: Society
sections.intro: Family, caste, gender, education and the move from village to city have shaped how Indians live together, and continue to change.

exhibits.title: Caste system
exhibits.text: Caste combines the four varnas with thousands of jatis, often linked to occupation and marriage within the group. Reformers and Dr B. R. Ambedkar fought caste discrimination; the Constitution abolished untouchability in Article 17 and provided reservations.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Dr B. R. Ambedkar

exhibits.title: The Indian family
exhibits.text: The joint family, with several generations living together, was traditionally common, especially in villages and among landowning groups. Urbanisation has increased nuclear families, though family ties remain strong.
exhibits.show: Late-19th/early-20th-century studio group portrait of a multi-generation Indian family

exhibits.title: Marriage in India
exhibits.text: Marriages are often arranged by families and usually within the community, with diverse rituals across regions and faiths. Laws such as the Special Marriage Act of 1954 and the Hindu Marriage Act of 1955 govern marriage, and child marriage is prohibited.
exhibits.show: Wedding procession of Dara Shikoh, Mughal painting (c. 1633–1740 versions)

exhibits.title: Women in Indian history
exhibits.text: Women's status has varied over time, from scholars such as Gargi in Vedic texts to restrictions in later periods, and leaders such as Rani Lakshmibai, Sarojini Naidu and Indira Gandhi. The law now guarantees equal rights, and a third of seats in local bodies are reserved for women.
exhibits.show: Portrait of Sarojini Naidu, first woman President of the INC (1925)

exhibits.title: Education through history
exhibits.text: From gurukuls and ancient universities such as Takshashila and Nalanda to madrasas, missionary schools and modern universities, education has steadily expanded. The Right to Education Act of 2009 made schooling free and compulsory for children aged six to fourteen.
exhibits.show: Ruins of Nalanda Mahavihara, Bihar (UNESCO site)

exhibits.title: Tribal communities
exhibits.text: India has more than seven hundred Scheduled Tribes, or Adivasi communities, about one in twelve Indians, including the Gonds, Bhils, Santhals and Nagas. Leaders such as Birsa Munda resisted colonial exploitation, and the Constitution protects tribal areas.
exhibits.show: The only known photograph of Birsa Munda (c. 1900, in custody)

exhibits.title: Urbanisation
exhibits.text: From Harappan cities to medieval capitals and colonial port cities like Bombay, Calcutta and Madras, cities have shaped India. Today about a third of Indians live in urban areas, and cities drive much of the economy.
exhibits.show: Victoria Terminus (now CSMT), Bombay, 1880s–1890s photograph

exhibits.title: Rural society
exhibits.text: Most Indians have historically lived in villages organised around agriculture, caste and kinship. Panchayati Raj, given constitutional status in 1992, brought elected local government to every village.
exhibits.show: A gram sabha / village panchayat meeting in session

quiz.q: Which article of the Constitution abolished untouchability?
quiz.why: Article 17 abolished untouchability.

quiz.q: The Right to Education Act of 2009 made schooling free and compulsory for children of which ages?
quiz.why: The Act covers children aged six to fourteen.

quiz.q: In which year was Panchayati Raj given constitutional status?
quiz.why: Panchayati Raj gained constitutional status in 1992.

sections.title: Historiography
sections.intro: How do we know about India's past, and who tells its story? This section looks at sources and at how historians' interpretations have changed.

exhibits.title: Ancient sources
exhibits.text: Knowledge of ancient India comes from literary sources, such as the Vedas, the epics, the Puranas, Buddhist and Jain texts, Sangam poetry and works like the Arthashastra, and from archaeology, inscriptions and coins.
exhibits.show: Rigveda manuscript page in Devanagari (19th-century copy)

exhibits.title: Archaeology
exhibits.text: Archaeology recovers the past from material remains. The Archaeological Survey of India was founded in 1861, with Alexander Cunningham as its first director, and excavations at Harappa, Taxila and many other sites transformed our understanding of history.
exhibits.show: 1920s ASI excavation photograph of Mohenjo-daro (Sir John Marshall era)

exhibits.title: Epigraphy
exhibits.text: Inscriptions on rock, pillars, copper plates and temple walls are vital records. James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837, unlocking Ashoka's edicts, and copper-plate land grants record rulers, villages and taxes.
exhibits.show: Chola copper-plate grant on its ring with royal seal (e.g. the Leiden plates)

exhibits.title: Numismatics
exhibits.text: The study of coins reveals rulers' names and dates, religion, trade and economic conditions. Indo-Greek and Kushana coins helped historians reconstruct dynasties that are otherwise little known.
exhibits.show: Bilingual silver drachm of Menander I (Greek and Kharosthi legends)

exhibits.title: Foreign travellers
exhibits.text: Visitors left valuable accounts: Megasthenes at the Mauryan court, the Buddhist pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang, Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind, Ibn Battuta in the Tughlaq period, and Europeans such as Bernier and Tavernier under the Mughals.
exhibits.show: Painting of Xuanzang carrying sutras on a backpack frame (Japanese/Chinese scroll)

exhibits.title: Colonial historians
exhibits.text: British writers such as James Mill, in his History of British India of 1817, divided Indian history into Hindu, Muslim and British periods and portrayed India as unchanging. Orientalists such as William Jones, by contrast, admired Indian learning.
exhibits.show: Title page of James Mill's The History of British India (1817)

exhibits.title: Nationalist historians
exhibits.text: Nationalist historians such as R. C. Majumdar, K. P. Jayaswal and R. K. Mookerji highlighted India's achievements, ancient traditions of self-government and cultural unity, countering colonial narratives.
exhibits.show: Photographic portrait of R. C. Majumdar (with Jayaswal's 'Hindu Polity' title page)

exhibits.title: Marxist historians
exhibits.text: Marxist historians such as D. D. Kosambi, R. S. Sharma, Irfan Habib and Romila Thapar studied economic structures, class and social change, including the debate over Indian feudalism in the early medieval period.
exhibits.show: Portrait of D. D. Kosambi (1907–1966)

exhibits.title: Subaltern studies
exhibits.text: Subaltern Studies, begun by Ranajit Guha in 1982, wrote history from below, focusing on peasants, workers, tribal communities and women rather than elites, and challenged both colonial and nationalist narratives.
exhibits.show: Illustrated London News engraving of the Santhal rebellion, 1855

exhibits.title: Contemporary interpretations
exhibits.text: Historians today use many methods, from ancient DNA and environmental history to gender, caste and regional studies and digital archives. Debates continue, and history remains a living conversation about evidence.
exhibits.show: Excavation of skeletons at Rakhigarhi, Haryana (source of the 2019 ancient-DNA study)

quiz.why: James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837, unlocking Ashoka's edicts.

quiz.why: Alexander Cunningham was the ASI's first director.

quiz.q: Which historian began Subaltern Studies in 1982?
quiz.why: Ranajit Guha began Subaltern Studies in 1982.
